column2: Participate in caring for your body and promoting your well-being.
Move body parts to express emotions, needs, and desires.
Imitate gestures and movements of other children, adults, and animals.
Experiment the bodily possibilities in play and interactions in welcoming and challenging environments.
Use grasping, fitting, and throwing movements, expanding your ability to handle different materials and objects.
Recognize when you are called by your name and recognize the names of people you live with.
Show interest when listening to the reading of poems and the presentation of music.
Show interest when listening to stories read or told, by looking at illustrations and watching the adult reader’s reading movements (how they hold the book and turn the pages).
Recognize elements of story illustrations, pointing them out at the request of the adult reader.
Imitate the variations in intonation and gestures made by adults when reading stories and when singing.
Communicate with other people using movements, gestures, babbles, speech, and other forms of expression.
Know and manipulate printed and audiovisual materials on different media (book, magazine, comic, newspaper, poster, CD, tablet, etc.).
Participate in listening situations of texts in different textual genres (poems, fables, stories, recipes, comics, advertisements, etc.).
Know and manipulate different writing instruments and supports.
Understand that your actions have effects on other children and adults.
Perceive the possibilities and limits of one's body in the games and interactions in which one participates.
Interact with children of the same age group and adults while exploring spaces, materials, objects, and toys.
Communicate needs, desires, and emotions, using gestures, babbling, and words.
Recognize your body and express your sensations during moments of eating, hygiene, play, and rest.
Interact with other children of the same age group and adults, adapting to social interaction.
Explore and discover the properties of objects and materials (odor, color, taste, temperature).
Explore cause-and-effect relationships (overflowing, dyeing, mixing, moving and removing, etc.) in interactions with the physical world.
Explore the environment through action and observation, manipulating, experimenting, and making discoveries.
Manipulate, experiment, arrange, and explore space through experiences of moving oneself and objects.
Manipulate various and diverse materials to compare the differences and similarities among them.
Experience different rhythms, speeds, and flows in interactions and play (in dances, swings, slides, etc.).
Explore sounds produced with one's own body and with objects in the environment.
Trace graphic marks on different supports using scratching instruments and paints.
Explore different sound sources and materials to accompany sung games, songs, music, and melodies.
Adopt gestures and movements from one's culture in self‑care and in games and play.
Move your body in space, orienting yourself by notions such as forward, backward, up, down, inside, outside, etc., when engaging in games and activities of different natures.
Explore ways of moving through space (jumping, leaping, dancing), combining movements and following instructions.
Demonstrate progressive independence in caring for one's body.
Develop progressively manual skills, acquiring control to draw, paint, tear, flip, among others.
Engage in dialogue with children and adults, expressing your desires, needs, feelings, and opinions.
Identify and create different sounds and recognize rhymes and alliterations in circle songs and poetic texts.

Show interest and attention when listening to the reading of stories and other texts, distinguishing written text from illustrations, and following, with guidance from the adult reader, the direction of reading (top to bottom, left to right).
Formulate and answer questions about facts from the narrated story, identifying settings, characters, and main events.
Report experiences and events that have occurred, stories heard, films or theatrical plays watched, etc.
Create and tell stories orally, based on images or suggested themes.
Handle different textual carriers, demonstrating recognition of their social uses.
Manipulate texts and participate in listening situations to broaden your contact with different textual genres (folk tales, adventure stories, comics, classroom posters, menus, news, etc.).
Use different writing instruments and supports to draw, trace letters, and other graphic signs.
Demonstrate caring and solidarity attitudes in interactions with children and adults.
Demonstrate a positive self-image and confidence in one's ability to face difficulties and challenges.
Share objects and spaces with children of the same age group and adults.
Communicate with peers and adults, seeking to understand them and to be understood.
Recognize that people have different physical characteristics, respecting those differences.
Respect basic rules of social coexistence in interactions and play.
Resolve conflicts in interactions and play, with the guidance of an adult.
Explore and describe similarities and differences between the characteristics and properties of objects (texture, mass, size).
Observe, report, and describe everyday incidents and natural phenomena (solar light, wind, rain, etc.).
Share, with other children, situations of caring for plants and animals in the institution’s spaces and outside it.
Identify spatial relationships (inside and outside, above, below, between, and next to) and temporal relationships (before, during, and after).
Classify objects, taking into account a given attribute (size, weight, color, shape, etc.).
Use basic time concepts (now, before, during, after, yesterday, today, tomorrow, slow, fast, quickly, slowly).
Count orally objects, people, books, etc., in various contexts.
Record the number of children (girls and boys, present and absent) and the number of objects of the same type (dolls, balls, books, etc.).
Create sounds with materials, objects, and musical instruments to accompany various music rhythms.
Use a variety of manipulable materials (clay, modeling dough), exploring colors, textures, surfaces, planes, shapes, and volumes while creating three‑dimensional objects.
Use different sound sources available in the environment in sung play, songs, music, and melodies.
Create with the body diversified forms of expression of feelings, sensations, and emotions, both in everyday situations and in play, dance, theater, and music.
Demonstrate control and appropriate use of one's body in play and games, listening and retelling stories, artistic activities, among other possibilities.
Create movements, gestures, looks, and mimics in play, games, and artistic activities such as dance, theater, and music.
Adopt self‑care habits related to hygiene, nutrition, comfort, and appearance.
Coordinate your manual skills to provide appropriate care that meets your interests and needs in various situations.
Express ideas, desires, and feelings about their experiences through oral and written language (spontaneous writing), photos, drawings, and other forms of expression.
Invent sung games, poems, and songs, creating rhymes, alliterations, and rhythms.
Choose and flip through books, looking for guidance by themes and illustrations, and trying to identify familiar words.
Retell stories that have been heard and collaboratively plan scripts for videos and performances, defining the settings, characters, and story structure.
Retell stories that have been heard in order to produce a written retelling, with the teacher acting as scribe.
Produce your own oral and written stories (spontaneous writing) in situations with significant social function.
Raise hypotheses about textual genres transmitted in familiar media, using graphic observation and/or reading strategies.
Select books and texts of familiar genres for an adult's reading and/or for one's own reading (drawing on one's repertoire of these texts, such as memory recall, reading the illustrations, etc.).
Raise hypotheses about written language by recording words and texts through spontaneous writing.
Show empathy for others, recognizing that people have different feelings, needs, and ways of thinking and acting.
Act independently, with confidence in your abilities, recognizing your achievements and limitations.
Expand interpersonal relationships, developing attitudes of participation and cooperation.
Communicate your ideas and feelings to diverse people and groups.
Show appreciation for the characteristics of your own body and respect the characteristics of others (children and adults) with whom you live.
Show interest and respect for different cultures and ways of life.
Use strategies based on mutual respect to deal with conflicts in interactions with children and adults.
Establish comparison relationships between objects by observing their properties.
Observe and describe changes in different materials, resulting from actions on them, in experiments involving natural and artificial phenomena.
Identify and select sources of information to answer questions about nature, its phenomena, and its conservation.
Record observations, manipulations, and measurements, using multiple languages (drawing, recording with numbers, or spontaneous writing), on different media.
Classify objects and figures according to their similarities and differences.
Report important facts about your birth and development, the history of your family, and your community.
Relate numbers to their respective quantities and identify the before, after, and between in a sequence.
Express measurements (weight, height, etc.) by constructing basic graphs.
Use sounds produced by materials, objects, and musical instruments during make‑believe play, performances, musical creations, and parties.
Express oneself freely through drawing, painting, collage, folding, and sculpture, creating two‑dimensional and three‑dimensional works.
Recognize the qualities of sound (intensity, duration, pitch, and timbre), using them in your sound productions and when listening to music and sounds.
Recognize that texts are read and written from left to right and from top to bottom of the page.
Write, spontaneously or by dictation, words and sentences alphabetically – using letters/graphemes that represent phonemes.
Observe conventional writings, comparing them to your own written productions, noticing similarities and differences.
Distinguish alphabet letters from other graphic signs.
Recognize the alphabetic writing system as a representation of the sounds of speech.
Orally segment words into syllables.
Identify phonemes and their representation by letters.
Relate sound elements (syllables, phonemes, parts of words) to their written representation.
Compare words, identifying similarities and differences between the sounds of their initial syllables.
Name the letters of the alphabet and recite them in order.
Know, differentiate, and relate letters in print and cursive format, uppercase and lowercase.
Recognize the separation of words in writing by blank spaces.
Compare words, identifying similarities and differences between sounds of medial and final syllables.
Identify other signs in the text besides letters, such as full stops, question marks, and exclamation marks, and their effects on intonation.
Group words by the criterion of similarity of meaning (synonymy) and separate words by the criterion of opposition of meaning (antonymy).

Read and understand, in collaboration with classmates and with the teacher’s help, quatrains, short quatrains, rhymes, tongue‑twisters, among other everyday life genres, taking into account the communicative situation and the text’s topic/theme, and relating its organizational form to its purpose.

Plan and produce, in collaboration with classmates and with the teacher’s help, lists, agendas, calendars, notices, invitations, recipes, assembly instructions, and captions for albums, photos, or illustrations (digital or printed), among other everyday life genres, taking into account the communicative situation and the theme/topic/purpose of the text.

Register, in collaboration with classmates and with the help of the teacher, songs, quatrains, little quatrains, rhymes, tongue‑twisters, among other genres of everyday life, considering the communicative situation and the theme/topic/purpose of the text.
Recite rhymes, quatrains, short quatrains, and tongue‑twisters with appropriate intonation and while observing the rhymes.

Identify and reproduce, in lists, agendas, calendars, rules, notices, invitations, recipes, assembly instructions, and captions for albums, photos, or illustrations (digital or printed), the specific formatting and layout of each of these genres.

Write, in collaboration with classmates and with the help of the teacher, lists of rules and regulations that organize life in the school community, among other genres in the field of civic action, considering the communicative situation and the theme/topic of the text.

Plan and produce, in collaboration with peers and with the help of the teacher, diagrams, interviews, curiosities, among other investigative field genres, digital or printed, considering the communicative situation and the theme/topic/purpose of the text.

Plan and produce, in collaboration with classmates and with the teacher’s help, interviews, curiosities, among other investigative genres, that can be orally transmitted using digital tools, in audio or video, taking into account the communicative situation and the text’s topic/theme/purpose.
Identify and reproduce, in school task statements, diagrams, interviews, curiosities, digital or printed, the specific formatting and layout of each of these genres, including their oral versions.

Produce, with the teacher acting as scribe, retellings of stories read by the teacher, stories imagined or based on picture books, observing the way of composing narrative texts (characters, plot, time, and space).
Identify elements of a narrative read or heard, including characters, plot, time, and space.
Read new words accurately by decoding; for frequently used words, read them holistically by memorization.
Search for, select, and read, with the teacher’s mediation (shared reading), texts that circulate in print or digital media, according to needs and interests.
Copy brief texts, preserving their characteristics and referring back to the text whenever you have doubts about its graphic layout, spacing between words, spelling of words, and punctuation.

Read and understand, in collaboration with classmates and with the help of the teacher or already with some autonomy, lists, agendas, calendars, notices, invitations, recipes, assembly instructions (digital or printed), among other everyday life genres, taking into account the communicative situation and the topic/theme of the text and relating its organizational form to its purpose.

Plan and produce, in collaboration with classmates and with the teacher’s help, (re)counts of stories, poems and other versified texts (song lyrics, short rhymes, folk tales), visual poems, strips and comic stories, among other artistic‑literary genres, taking into account the communicative situation and the purpose of the text.

Plan and produce, in collaboration with classmates and with the teacher’s help, messages, notices, invitations, recipes, assembly instructions, among other everyday life genres, that can be orally transmitted using digital tools, in audio or video, taking into account the communicative situation and the text’s topic/purpose.

Identify and (re)produce, in chants, quatrains, short quatrains, rhymes, tongue‑twisters, and songs, the use of rhymes, alliterations, assonances, and the rhythm of speech related to the rhythm and melody of music and their effects on meaning.

Read and understand, in collaboration with classmates and with the teacher’s help, photo captions in news, headlines and lead paragraphs in news, digital photo news albums, and short news for children, among other journalistic genres, taking into account the communicative situation and the topic/theme of the text.

Read and understand, in collaboration with classmates and with the teacher’s help, slogans, advertising copy, and public awareness campaign texts aimed at children, among other advertising genres, taking into account the communicative situation and the theme/topic of the text.

Read and understand, in collaboration with classmates and with the teacher’s help, posters, notices, flyers, rules and regulations that organize life in the school community, among other civic‑action genres, taking into account the communicative situation and the topic/theme of the text.

Write, in collaboration with classmates and with the help of the teacher, photo captions for news, headlines and lead paragraphs in news, a digital news photo album, and short news for a child audience, in digital or print formats, among other journalistic genres, taking into account the communicative situation and the theme/topic of the text.

Write, in collaboration with classmates and with the help of the teacher, slogans, advertising copy, and awareness campaign texts aimed at a child audience, among other advertising genres, taking into account the communicative situation and the theme/topic/purpose of the text.

Plan, in collaboration with classmates and with the teacher’s help, slogans and a public‑awareness campaign piece aimed at children that can be orally delivered using digital tools, audio or video, taking into account the communicative situation and the text’s topic/purpose.

Identify and reproduce, in photo captions of news, digital news photo albums, reader letters (children’s magazine), digital or printed, the specific formatting and layout of each of these genres, including their oral versions.
Identify the composition method of advertising slogans.

Identify and reproduce, in advertising announcements and awareness‑campaign texts aimed at children (oral and written, digital or printed), the specific formatting and layout of each of these genres, including the use of images.

Read and understand, in collaboration with classmates and with the help of the teacher, statements of school tasks, diagrams, curiosities, short experiment reports, interviews, child encyclopedia entries, among other investigative genre texts, taking into account the communicative situation and the topic/theme of the text.
Appreciate poems and other versified texts, observing rhymes, sounds, wordplay, recognizing their belonging to the imaginary world and their dimension of enchantment, play, and enjoyment.
Recognize, in verse texts, rhymes, sounds, wordplay, words, expressions, and comparisons, relating them to sensations and associations.

Identify the social function of texts that circulate in everyday social spheres (home, street, community, school) and in printed, mass, and digital media, recognizing why they were produced, where they circulate, who produced them, and who they are intended for.

Establish expectations about the text you are about to read (anticipatory assumptions about meaning, form, and the text’s social function), relying on your prior knowledge of the conditions of production and reception of that text, its genre, medium, and thematic universe, as well as on textual highlights, graphic resources, images, and data from the work itself (index, preface, etc.), confirming the anticipations and inferences made before and during reading, and checking the adequacy of the hypotheses made.
Locate explicit information in texts.
Identify the effect on meaning produced by using graphic‑visual expressive resources in multisemiotic texts.

Plan, with the teacher’s help, the text to be produced, taking into account the communicative situation, the interlocutors (who writes/for whom the writing is intended); the purpose or goal (why write); the circulation (where the text will circulate); the medium (what carries the text); the language, organization, and form of the text and its topic, researching printed or digital sources whenever necessary for information needed for the text production, organizing the data and researched sources into topics.

Read and revise the text produced with the help of the teacher and the collaboration of classmates, correcting and improving it by making cuts, additions, reformulations, and corrections of spelling and punctuation.
Edit the final version of the text, collaborating with classmates and with the teacher’s help, illustrating when appropriate in an appropriate manual or digital support.
Use software, including word‑processing programs, to edit and publish the texts produced, exploring the available multisemiotic resources.
Express yourself in oral exchange situations with clarity, focusing on being understood by the interlocutor and using words with an audible voice tone, good articulation, and appropriate rhythm.
Listen attentively to teachers and classmates, formulating relevant questions about the topic and requesting clarifications whenever necessary.

Recognize the characteristics of spontaneous face‑to‑face conversation, respecting turns of speaking, and selecting and using, during the conversation, appropriate forms of address according to the situation and the interlocutor’s position.

Assign meaning to non‑linguistic (paralinguistic) aspects observed in speech, such as eye direction, laughter, gestures, head movements (agreement or disagreement), body expression, and tone of voice.
Identify the purposes of oral interaction in different communicative contexts (requesting information, presenting opinions, informing, reporting experiences, etc.).
Build the sense of comics and strips, relating images and words and interpreting graphic resources (types of balloons, lettering, onomatopoeias).
Recognize that literary texts are part of the world of imagination and present a playful, enchanting dimension, valuing them, in their cultural diversity, as humanity's artistic heritage.

Read and understand, in collaboration with classmates and with the teacher’s help and later independently, longer narrative texts such as stories (folk, fairy tales, cumulative, spooky, etc.) and chronicles.
Appreciate visual and concrete poems, observing the sense effects created by the text’s format on the page, the distribution and layout of the letters, the illustrations, and other visual effects.
Relate text with illustrations and other graphic resources.
Retell orally, with and without visual support, literary texts read by the teacher.

Use correct spelling of known words or words with syllabic structures already mastered, capital letters at the beginning of sentences and in proper nouns, spacing between words, a period, a question mark, and an exclamation point.
Segment words into syllables and remove and replace initial, medial, or final syllables to create new words.
Read and write words with regular direct letter‑to‑phoneme correspondences (f, v, t, d, p, b) and with regular contextual correspondences (c and q; e and o, when in unstressed final position).
Read and write correctly words with CV, V, CVC, and CCV syllables, identifying that there are vowels in every syllable.
Read and write correctly words with nasalization marks (tilde, m, n).
Understand the acrophonic principle that operates in the names of the letters of the alphabet.
Write words, sentences, and short texts in print and cursive forms.
Segment words correctly when writing sentences and texts.
Use the period, question mark, and exclamation point appropriately.
Identify synonyms of words in the read text, determining the difference in meaning between them, and form antonyms of words found in the read text by adding the negation prefix in-/im-.
Form the augmentative and diminutive of words with the suffixes -ão and -inho/-zinho.

Read and understand, with a certain degree of autonomy, songs, song lyrics, and other everyday life genres, taking into account the communicative situation and the theme or subject of the text, and relating its organizational form to its purpose.
Plan and produce tickets and letters, in printed and/or digital media, among other everyday life genres, taking into account the communicative situation and the theme/topic/purpose of the text.

Plan and produce short observation reports of processes, facts, and personal experiences, maintaining the characteristics of the genre, while considering the communicative situation and the theme/topic of the text.
Sing songs and chants, following the rhythm and melody.
Identify and reproduce, in notes, messages, notices, letters, emails, recipes (how-to), reports (digital or printed), the specific formatting and layout of each of these genres.

Identify and reproduce, in personal experience narratives, the sequence of events, using expressions that indicate the passage of time (“before”, “after”, “yesterday”, “today”, “tomorrow”, “another day”, “in the past”, “a long time ago”, etc.), and the necessary level of informativeness.

Plan and produce posters and flyers to promote school or community events, using persuasive language and appropriate textual and visual elements (font size, layout, images) for the genre, taking into account the communicative situation and the topic/theme of the text.

Plan and produce, in collaboration with classmates and with the teacher’s help, short news pieces for a child audience, to compose a spoken newspaper that can be delivered orally or in a digital medium, in audio or video, among other journalistic genres, taking into account the communicative situation and the topic/theme of the text.
Recognize the function of texts used to present information collected in research activities (surveys, short interviews, records of experiments).
Explore, with the teacher’s mediation, informational texts from various digital research environments, learning about their possibilities.

Plan and produce, in collaboration with classmates and with the teacher’s help, short accounts of experiments, interviews, child encyclopedia entries, among other investigative genres, in digital or printed form, taking into account the communicative situation and the text’s topic/theme/purpose.
Plan and produce, with a certain degree of autonomy, small observation records of research results that are consistent with an investigated topic.

Plan and produce, in collaboration with classmates and with the teacher’s help, reports of experiments, observation logs, interviews, among other investigative genres, that can be orally presented using digital tools, in audio or video, taking into account the communicative situation and the text’s topic/purpose.

Identify and reproduce, in reports of experiments, interviews, children's encyclopedia entries, digital or printed, the specific formatting and layout of each of these genres, including their oral versions.
Read and understand, with a certain degree of autonomy, literary texts of various genres, developing a taste for reading.
Rewrite literary narrative texts read by the teacher.
Recognize the conflict that generates a fictional narrative and its resolution, as well as words, expressions, and phrases that characterize characters and settings.
Observe, in visual poems, the text format on the page, the illustrations, and other visual effects.

Read and write words with regular contextual correspondences between graphemes and phonemes – c/qu; g/gu; r/rr; s/ss; o (and not u) and e (and not i) in an unstressed syllable at the end of a word – and with nasalization marks (tilde, m, n).
Read and write correctly words with syllables CV, V, CVC, CCV, VC, VV, CVV, identifying that there are vowels in all syllables.
Read and write correctly words with the digraphs lh, nh, ch.
Use an acute or circumflex accent on stressed monosyllables that end in a, e, or o, and on oxytone words that end in a, e, or o, whether or not they are followed by an s.
Identify the number of syllables in words, classifying them as monosyllables, disyllables, trisyllables, and polysyllables.
Identify the stressed syllable in words, classifying them as oxytone, paroxytone, and proparoxytone.
Identify the function in reading and use in writing the period, question mark, exclamation point, and in dialogues (direct speech), the colon and dash.
Identify and differentiate, in texts, nouns and verbs and their functions in the sentence: agent, action, object of the action.
Identify, in texts, adjectives and their function of attributing properties to nouns.
Recognize productive prefixes and suffixes in the formation of derived words from nouns, adjectives, and verbs, using them to understand words and to form new words.

Read and understand, independently, instructional directive texts (recipes, assembly instructions, etc.), with the specific structure of these texts (imperative verbs, step‑by‑step instructions) and blending words, images, and graphic‑visual resources, taking into account the communicative situation and the topic/theme of the text.

Read and understand, independently, personal letters and diaries, expressing feelings and opinions, among other everyday life genres, in accordance with the conventions of the letter genre and taking into account the communicative situation and the theme or subject of the text.

Plan and produce personal letters and diaries, expressing feelings and opinions, among other everyday life genres, in accordance with the conventions of the letter and diary forms and taking into account the communicative situation and the theme/topic of the text.

Plan and produce instructional imperative texts, using the specific structure of these texts (imperative verbs, step-by-step instructions) and blending words, images, and graphic-visual resources, taking into account the communicative situation and the topic/subject of the text.
Watch a digital video of a children’s cooking program and, based on it, plan and produce recipes in audio or video.

Identify and reproduce, in instructional imperative texts (recipes, assembly instructions, digital or printed), the specific formatting of these texts (imperative verbs, indication of steps to be followed) and the particular layout of texts in these genres (list of ingredients or materials and execution instructions – “how to do it”).

Identify and reproduce, in epistolary and diary genres, the specific formatting of these texts (accounts of events, expression of experiences, emotions, opinions or criticisms) and the particular layout of texts in these genres (date, greeting, body of the text, farewell, signature).

Read and understand, independently, letters addressed to print or digital media outlets (reader letters and complaint letters to newspapers, magazines) and news, among other journalistic genres, in accordance with the conventions of the letter genre and taking into account the communicative situation and the topic/subject of the text.
Identify and discuss the purpose of using persuasive resources (colors, images, word choice, word play, font size) in advertising and propaganda texts, as elements of convincing.

Produce letters addressed to print or digital media outlets (reader letters or complaint letters to newspapers or magazines), among other political-citizen genre texts, with opinions and criticisms, in accordance with the conventions of the letter genre and considering the communicative situation and the theme/subject of the text.

Produce advertising announcements and awareness campaign texts aimed at children, observing the persuasive techniques used in advertising and propaganda texts (colors, images, slogans, word choice, word play, font size and type, layout).

Plan and produce, in collaboration with classmates, a children's news program featuring some news and campaign texts that can be delivered orally or through digital media, in audio or video, taking into account the communicative situation, the specific organization of speech in these genres, and the theme/topic/purpose of the texts.
Analyze the use of adjectives in letters addressed to media outlets, whether printed or digital (such as reader letters or complaint letters to newspapers or magazines).
Read/listen and understand, independently, accounts of observations and research from information sources, taking into account the communicative situation and the theme/topic of the text.

Plan and produce texts to present results of observations and research in information sources, including, when relevant, images, diagrams, graphs, or simple tables, taking into account the communicative situation and the theme/topic of the text.

Identify and reproduce, in observation and research reports, the specific formatting and layout of these genres (steps or item lists, tables, illustrations, graphs, summary of results), including their oral versions.
Recite cordel and sing repentes and emboladas, observing the rhymes and following the rhythm and melody.
Read and understand, silently and then aloud, with autonomy and fluency, short texts with an appropriate level of textuality.

Select books from the library and/or the classroom reading corner and/or available in digital media for individual reading, justifying the choice and sharing with classmates their opinion after the reading.
Identify the central idea of the text, demonstrating overall comprehension.
Infer implicit information from the texts read.
Infer the meaning of unknown words or expressions in texts, based on the context of the sentence or text.

Recover relationships between parts of a text, identifying lexical substitutions (replacing nouns with synonyms) or pronominal substitutions (using anaphoric pronouns—personal, possessive, demonstrative) that contribute to the continuity of the text.

Use linguistic and grammatical knowledge when producing a text, such as spelling, basic rules of nominal and verbal agreement, punctuation (full stop, exclamation point, question mark, commas in enumerations), and punctuation of direct speech, when applicable.

Use, when producing a text, referencing resources (by lexical substitution or by personal, possessive, and demonstrative pronouns), vocabulary appropriate to the genre, pronominal cohesion resources (anaphoric pronouns), and articulators of sense relations (time, cause, opposition, conclusion, comparison), with a sufficient level of informativeness.
Organize the text into units of meaning, dividing it into paragraphs according to graphic norms and in accordance with the characteristics of the text genre.

Identify the genres of oral discourse used in different communicative situations and contexts, and their linguistic‑expressive and compositional characteristics (spontaneous conversation, telephone conversation, personal interviews, radio or TV interviews, debate, radio and TV news, sports game narration on radio and TV, classroom, debate, etc.).

Listen to recordings, songs, and spoken texts in different linguistic varieties, identifying regional, urban, and rural speech characteristics and respecting the diverse linguistic varieties as features of language use by different regional groups or local cultures, rejecting linguistic prejudice.
Use the dictionary to clarify doubts about how to write words, especially when the words have irregular phoneme‑grapheme relationships.
Memorize the spelling of frequently used words in which the phoneme‑grapheme relationships are irregular and that begin with an h that does not represent a phoneme.
Identify personal, possessive, and demonstrative pronouns in texts and use them in written production as an anaphoric cohesive device.

Express and defend a viewpoint on a controversial topic related to situations experienced in school and/or the community, using a formal register and an appropriate argumentative structure, taking into account the communicative situation and the topic/subject of the text.

Identify and reproduce, in news, headlines, leads, and simple news bodies for a child audience, as well as complaint letters (children’s magazine), whether digital or printed, the specific formatting and layout of each of these genres, including their oral versions.
Search for and select, with the teacher’s support, information of interest about social and natural phenomena in texts that circulate in print or digital media.
Listen attentively to presentations of work performed by colleagues, formulating relevant questions about the topic and requesting clarifications whenever necessary.
Retrieve the main ideas in formal listening situations of exhibitions, presentations, and lectures.

Present school projects or research in the classroom, using multisemiotic resources (images, diagrams, tables, etc.), guided by a written outline, planning speaking time and adapting language to the communicative situation.
Read and understand, independently, literary texts of various genres and lengths, including those without illustrations, forming preferences for genres, themes, and authors.
Understand dialogues in narrative texts, noting the sense effect of enunciative verbs and, if applicable, the use of linguistic varieties in direct speech.
Appreciate poems and other versified texts, observing rhymes, alliterations, and different ways of dividing verses, stanzas, and refrains and their effect on meaning.
Identify the functions of a dramatic text (written to be staged) and its organization through dialogues between characters and markers of the characters' speeches and scenes.

Create fictional narratives, with a certain degree of autonomy, using descriptive details, sequences of events, and appropriate images to support the sense of the text, as well as markers of time, space, and character dialogue.

Read and understand, with some autonomy, fictional narratives that present settings and characters, observing the elements of narrative structure: plot, time, space, characters, narrator, and the construction of indirect discourse and direct discourse.
Read and understand, with some autonomy, texts in verse, exploring rhymes, sounds and word play, poetic images (figurative senses) and visual and sonic resources.
Recite poems with appropriate intonation, posture, and interpretation.

Identify in narratives the setting, central character, conflict that drives the story, resolution, and the point of view from which the stories are narrated, distinguishing narratives in first and third person.
Differentiate indirect speech and direct speech, determining the sense effect of enunciation verbs and explaining the use of linguistic varieties in direct speech, when applicable.
Identify, in verse texts, the sense effects that arise from the use of rhythmic and sonic resources and from metaphors.
Write words using regular direct and contextual phoneme‑grapheme correspondence rules.
Read and write correctly words with VV and CVV syllables in cases where the VV combination (diphthong) is reduced in spoken language (ai, ei, ou).
Locate words in the dictionary to clarify meanings, recognizing the most plausible meaning for the context that prompted the inquiry.
Use an acute or circumflex accent on paroxytone words that end in -i(s), -l, -r, or -ão(s).

Identify the function in reading and appropriately use in writing the period, question mark, exclamation point, colon, and dash in dialogues (direct speech), the comma in enumerations and in separating a vocative and an appositive.
Identify in texts and use in textual production the agreement between a noun or personal pronoun and the verb (verbal agreement).
Identify in texts and use in textual production the agreement between article, noun, and adjective (agreement in the nominal group).
Recognize and correctly write derived words with the suffixes -agem, -oso, -eza, -izar/-isar (regular morphological).

Read and understand, independently, invoices, bills, payment slips, and other everyday life documents, following the genre conventions (sections, listed items, consumption units, barcode) while taking into account the communicative context and the purpose of the text.

Read and understand, independently, personal complaint letters, among other everyday life genres, in accordance with the conventions of the letter genre and taking into account the communicative situation and the theme/topic/purpose of the text.

Plan and produce, independently, personal complaint letters, among other everyday‑life genres, in accordance with the conventions of the letter genre and the specific structure of these texts (problem, opinion, arguments), taking into account the communicative situation and the theme/topic/purpose of the text.
Watch a digital video of a children’s program that includes assembly instructions, games, and activities, and then plan and produce audio or video tutorials based on it.

Identify and reproduce, in instructional imperative texts (instructions for digital or printed games), the specific formatting of these texts (imperative verbs, indication of steps to follow) and the specific format of the oral or written texts of these genres (list/presentation of materials and game instructions/steps).
Identify, in news, the facts, participants, location, and time of the reported event.
Distinguish facts from opinions/suggestions in texts (informative, journalistic, advertising, etc.).

Produce news about events that occurred in the school environment, whether digital or printed, for the school newspaper, reporting the events and their actors and commenting on the consequences, in accordance with the conventions of the news genre and taking into account the communicative situation and the theme/topic of the text.

Produce radio or television news programs and interviews broadcast on radio, TV, and the internet, guided by a script or text, and demonstrating knowledge of spoken/television news genres and interview techniques.
Analyze the intonation pattern and facial and bodily expression of radio or television news anchors and of interviewers/interviewees.
Read and understand expository scientific popularization texts for children, taking into account the communicative situation and the theme/topic of the text.
Recognize the function of graphs, diagrams, and tables in texts as a way of presenting data and information.

Plan and produce texts on topics of interest, based on results of observations and research in printed or electronic information sources, including, when relevant, images and graphs or simple tables, considering the communicative situation and the topic/subject of the text.
Plan and produce, with some autonomy, encyclopedia entries for children—digital or printed—taking into account the communicative situation and the theme/subject/purpose of the text.

Identify and reproduce, in children's encyclopedia entries—whether digital or printed—the specific formatting and layout of this genre (entry title, definition, details, curiosities), taking into account the communicative situation and the text’s topic/theme/purpose.
Identify and reproduce, in their format, tables, diagrams, and graphs in observation and research reports, as a way of presenting data and information.
Represent scenes from dramatic texts, reproducing the characters' lines, in accordance with the interpretation and movement cues indicated by the author.
Observe, in concrete poems, the format, distribution, and layout of the letters of the text on the page.
Identify, in dramatic texts, markers of the characters' speech and of the scene.
Write words using regular phoneme‑grapheme correspondence rules, contextual and morphological rules, and frequent‑use words with irregular correspondences.

Identify the polysemous nature of words (the same word having different meanings depending on the context of use), by comparing the meaning of certain terms used in scientific fields with those same terms used in everyday language.
Accurately accentuate oxytone, paroxytone, and proparoxytone words.
Differentiate, when reading texts, the comma, semicolon, colon, and recognize, when reading texts, the sense effect that results from the use of ellipses, quotation marks, and parentheses.
Identify the expression of present, past, and future in indicative verb tenses.
Conjugate, appropriately, in writing and speaking, verbs in agreement with personal pronouns/subject nouns of the sentence.
Identify, in texts, the use of conjunctions and the relationship they establish between parts of the text: addition, opposition, time, cause, condition, purpose.
Differentiate primitive, derived, and compound words, and words derived by adding a prefix and a suffix.

Read and understand, independently, instructional texts of game rules, among other everyday life genres, in accordance with the genre conventions and taking into account the communicative situation and the text’s purpose.

Read and understand, independently, anecdotes, jokes, and cartoons, among other everyday life genres, in accordance with the conventions of the genre and taking into account the communicative situation and the purpose of the text.

Register, independently, anecdotes, jokes, and cartoons, among other everyday life genres, in accordance with genre conventions and taking into account the communicative situation and the text’s purpose.

Plan and produce, autonomously, instructional texts of game rules, among other everyday life genres, in accordance with the conventions of the genre and taking into account the communicative situation and the purpose of the text.
Watch a digital video of a children's vlog that reviews toys and children’s literature books, and then plan and produce digital audio or video reviews.
Identify and reproduce, in critical review texts of toys or children’s literature books, the specific formatting of those texts (presentation and product evaluation).

Read/watch and understand, independently, news, reports, videos in argumentative vlogs, among other political-civic genre texts, in accordance with genre conventions and considering the communicative situation and the text’s topic/subject.
Compare information about the same fact presented in different media and conclude which is more reliable and why.

Produce a script for editing a digital news report on topics of interest to the class, based on searches for information, images, audio, and video on the internet, in accordance with the conventions of the genre and considering the communicative situation and the theme/subject of the text.

Script, produce, and edit videos for argumentative vlogs about media products for children (films, cartoons, comics, games, etc.), based on knowledge of those products, following the conventions of the genre and taking into account the communicative situation and the topic/theme/purpose of the text.
Orally argue about socially relevant events, using knowledge of facts reported on TV, radio, print, and digital media, while respecting differing viewpoints.
Analyze the validity and strength of arguments in discussions about media products for children (films, cartoons, comics, games, etc.), based on knowledge about those products.
Analyze the intonation pattern, facial and body expression, and the choices of linguistic variety and register of vloggers of opinion or argumentative vlogs.
Read and understand dictionary entries, identifying the structure, grammatical information (meaning of abbreviations), and semantic information.
Compare information presented in graphs or tables.

Plan and produce a text on a topic of interest, organizing research results from printed or digital information sources, including images and graphics or tables, while considering the communicative situation and the theme or subject of the text.
Plan and produce, with a certain degree of autonomy, dictionary entries—digital or printed—taking into account the communicative situation and the theme/topic/purpose of the text.

Use, when producing the text, linguistic and grammatical knowledge: syntactic rules of nominal and verbal agreement, conventions for writing quotations, punctuation (full stop, colon, commas in enumerations), and orthographic rules.

Use, when producing the text, pronoun cohesion resources (anaphoric pronouns) and sense‑relation articulators (time, cause, opposition, conclusion, comparison), with an appropriate level of informativeness.
Observe the multisemiotic resources present in cyberpoems and children's micro-stories in digital media.

Recognize the impossibility of absolute neutrality in reporting facts and identify different degrees of bias/ impartiality given by the selection made and the sense effects arising from choices made by the author, in order to develop a critical attitude toward journalistic texts and become aware of the choices made while producing texts.
Establish a relationship between the different journalistic genres, understanding the centrality of the news.
Analyze differences in meaning between words in a synonymic series.
Analyze the function and inflections of nouns and adjectives and of verbs in the Indicative, Subjunctive, and Imperative moods: affirmative and negative.
Identify the sense effects of verbal moods, considering the text genre and communicative intention.

Employ, appropriately, the rules of nominal agreement (relations between nouns and their determiners) and the rules of verbal agreement (relations between the verb and the simple and compound subject).
Identify, in texts, compound sentences composed of clauses separated by commas without the use of connectors, naming them as compound sentences by coordination.
Identify, in a text or textual sequence, sentences as units constituted around a verbal nucleus and periods as a set of connected sentences.
Classify, in a text or textual sequence, the simple and compound sentences.
Identify nominal and verbal phrases as immediate constituents of the sentence.
Use linguistic and grammatical knowledge when producing text: verb tenses, nominal and verbal agreement, spelling rules, punctuation, etc.

Use, when producing text, referential cohesion resources (names and pronouns), semantic resources of synonymy, antonymy, and homonymy, and mechanisms for representing different voices (direct and indirect speech).
Analyze the structure and functioning of hyperlinks in news texts published on the Web and envision possibilities of hypertextual writing.

Explore the space reserved for the reader in newspapers, magazines, print and online media, news sites, etc., highlighting news, photo reports, interviews, cartoons, topics, themes, debates in focus, positioning oneself ethically and respectfully in front of these texts and related opinions, and publishing news, journalistic notes, general-interest photo reports in these reader spaces.
Compare information about the same fact presented in different media and outlets, analyzing and evaluating reliability.
Distinguish, in discontinuous segments of texts, the fact from the opinion expressed about that same fact.

Identify and evaluate explicit theses, opinions, positions, and arguments in argumentative texts (such as a letter to the editor, comment, opinion article, critical review, etc.), expressing agreement or disagreement.
Identify the sense effects caused by lexical selection, topicalization of elements, selection and hierarchy of information, use of third person, etc.

Identify the use of persuasive devices in various argumentative texts (such as title construction, lexical choices, metaphorical structures, the explicit or hidden presentation of information sources) and perceive their effects on meaning.

Identify the meaning effects caused by the choice of static images, sequencing or overlay of images, definition of foreground/background, angle, depth and focus, colors/tones, relationship with the text (reiteration, complement, or opposition) etc. in news, reports, photo‑journalism, photo‑exposés, memes, GIFs, advertising announcements and commercials published in newspapers, magazines, websites, etc.

Plan a printed news story and for distribution in other media (radio or TV/video), taking into account the production conditions of the text—purpose, readers/viewers, outlets and circulation media, etc.—starting from the choice of the fact to be reported (relevant to the class, school, or community), gathering data and information about the fact— which may involve interviews with participants or experts, consulting sources, analyzing documents, covering events, etc.—recording that information and data, selecting photos or images to produce or use, etc., and anticipating a hypertextual structure (in the case of publication on news sites or blogs).

Produce a printed news story taking into account the genre’s characteristics—headline with a verb in the present tense, optional byline, lead, progression given by descending order of importance of facts, use of third person, and words that indicate precision—and establish appropriate cohesion; and produce news for TV, radio, and the internet, taking into account, in addition to the genre’s characteristics, the available media resources and the handling of audio and visual capture and editing tools.

Plan reviews, vlogs, videos, and podcasts of various kinds, as well as texts and videos for presenting and appreciating youth cultures (some possibilities: fanzines, fanclips, e-zines, gameplay, detonado, etc.), among others, taking into account the conditions of text production – purpose, readers/viewers, distribution channels and media, etc. – by choosing a cultural production or event to analyze – book, film, series, game, song, music video, fanclip, show, saraus, slams, etc. – researching information about the chosen production or event, synthesizing information about the work/event and selecting aspects, elements, or resources that can be highlighted positively or negatively, or scripting the step-by-step process of the game for later video recording.

Produce critical reviews, vlogs, videos, podcasts, and other productions and genres from youth cultures (such as fanzines, fan clips, e-zines, gameplay, detonado, etc.) that present, describe, and/or evaluate cultural productions (book, film, series, game, song, album, music video, etc.) or events (show, sarau, slam, etc.), taking into account the given production context, the characteristics of the genre, the resources of the involved media, and the appropriate textualization of the texts and/or productions.

Produce, review, and edit advertising texts, taking into account the given production context, exploring multisemiotic resources, relating verbal and visual elements, appropriately using persuasive and/or convincing discourse strategies, and creating a title or slogan that motivates the reader to interact with the produced text and feels attracted to the service, idea, or product in question.

Define the context for producing the interview (objectives, what is intended to achieve, why that particular interviewee, etc.), gather information about the interviewee and about the event or topic in question, prepare the question script, and conduct an oral interview with involved parties or specialists related to the reported fact or the topic at hand, using a pre‑written script and formulating additional questions based on the answers given. When appropriate, select portions, transcribe, and edit the text into written form, adapting it to its publication context, to the compositional structure of the genre, and ensuring the relevance of the retained information and thematic continuity.

Identify the prohibition imposed or the right guaranteed, as well as the circumstances of its application, in articles related to school regulations, civil society statutes, advertising market regulations, the Consumer Defense Code, the National Traffic Code, the Child and Adolescent Statute, the Constitution, among others.

Explore and analyze spaces for rights complaints and request submissions (such as ombudsman offices, customer service centers, channels linked to public agencies, consumer platforms, complaint platforms), as well as texts belonging to genres that circulate in these spaces—complaint or complaint letter, request or request letter—in order to broaden the possibilities for producing these texts in cases that involve claims related to the school, the community, or its members, as a way to engage in seeking solutions to personal, others', and collective problems.

Analyze, based on the production context, the way in which request and complaint letters are organized (dating, opening style, contextualized presentation of the request or complaint, generally accompanied by explanations, arguments, and/or descriptions of the problem, a closing formula that is more or less cordial depending on the type of letter and signature) and some of the linguistic markers related to argumentation, explanation, or factual reporting, as a way to enable the grounded writing of such letters or posts on dedicated complaint and request channels in situations involving issues related to the school, the community, or any of its members.
Identify the object of the complaint and/or request and its support, explanation, or justification, so as to be able to analyze the pertinence of the request or justification.

Conduct a survey of issues and problems that require reporting of rights violations, claims, complaints, and requests that involve the school community or its members, and examine relevant rules and legislation.
Conduct research, starting from pre‑defined excerpts and questions, using both specified and open sources.
Disseminate research results through oral presentations, panels, science outreach articles, encyclopedia entries, scientific podcasts, etc.
Produce summaries, based on the notes and/or outlines made, using appropriate paraphrases and quotations.

Respect speaking turns when participating in conversations, discussions, or group activities in the classroom and at school, and formulate coherent and appropriate questions at suitable moments during classes, oral presentations, seminars, etc.

Take notes from classes, oral presentations, interviews (live, audio, TV, video), identifying and prioritizing the main information, with the aim of supporting study and the production of summaries and personal reflections or other related objectives.

Recognize and use the criteria for topical organization (from general to specific, from specific to general, etc.), the linguistic markers of that organization (ordering and enumeration markers, markers of explanation, definition, and exemplification, for example), and paraphrasing mechanisms, in order to better organize the cohesion and thematic progression of your texts.
Recognize the hypertext structure in scientific outreach texts and proceed to reference concepts and relationships through footnotes or boxes.

Analyze, among literary texts and between these and other artistic manifestations (such as cinema, theater, music, visual and media arts), explicit or implicit references to other texts, regarding themes, characters, and literary and semiotic resources.

Read independently and understand – selecting appropriate reading procedures and strategies for different purposes and taking into account the characteristics of genres and media – children’s and young adult novels, popular tales, horror stories, Brazilian, indigenous, and African legends, adventure narratives, mystery narratives, myths, chronicles, autobiographies, comic books, manga, free‑form and fixed‑form poems (such as sonnets and cordel), video poems, visual poems, among others, expressing evaluation of the text read and establishing preferences for genres, themes, and authors.
Identify, in a dramatic text, the character, act, scene, dialogue, stage directions, and the organization of the text: plot, conflicts, main ideas, points of view, and reference worlds.

Create fictional narratives, such as folk tales, suspense, mystery, horror, humor, puzzle stories, chronicles, comic strips, among others, that use realistic or fantasy settings and characters, observing the narrative structure elements appropriate to the intended genre, such as plot, characters, time, space, and narrator, using verb tenses suitable for narrating past events, and applying knowledge of different ways to start a story and to insert direct and indirect speech.
Form antonyms by adding prefixes that express a notion of negation.
Punctuate texts appropriately.

Create poems composed of free verses and fixed forms (such as quatrains and sonnets), using visual, semantic, and sonic resources, such as cadences, rhythms, and rhymes, as well as visual poems and video poems, exploring the relationships between image and verbal text, the distribution of the graphic stain (visual poem), and other visual and sonic resources.
Write words with correct spelling, following the conventions of written language.
Distinguish words derived by affixation and compound words.
Use, when producing text, referential cohesion resources (lexical and pronominal) and sequential cohesion, as well as other expressive resources appropriate to the text genre.
Analyze, in different texts, the sense effects that result from using linguistic‑discursive resources of prescription, causality, descriptive and expository sequences, and ordering of events.
Analyze the sense effects of using figures of speech, such as comparison, metaphor, metonymy, personification, hyperbole, among others.
Differentiate freedom of expression from hate speech, positioning oneself against this type of speech and envisioning possibilities of reporting when appropriate.

Analyze and compare various advertising pieces (posters, flyers, billboards, ads and commercials across different media, spots, jingles, videos, etc.) in order to perceive how they are coordinated within campaigns, the specific characteristics of the different semiotic systems and media, the suitability of these pieces for the target audience, the advertiser’s or campaign’s objectives, and the compositional construction and style of the genres in question, as a way to broaden their understanding (and production) of texts belonging to those genres.

Identify, in news stories, the central fact, its main circumstances, and any resulting consequences; in reports and photo reports, the fact or theme depicted and the perspective of the approach; in interviews, the main topics/subtopics discussed, explanations given or theses defended regarding those subtopics; in comics, memes, cartoons, the criticism, irony, or humor present.

Identify and analyze the sense‑forming effects that strengthen persuasion in advertising texts, relating persuasion strategies and appeals to consumption with the linguistic‑discourse resources used, such as images, verb tense, word play, figures of speech, etc., with the aim of fostering conscious consumption practices.

Infer and justify, in multisemiotic texts—such as comics, cartoons, memes, GIFs, etc.—the effect of humor, irony, and/or criticism that arises from the ambiguous use of words, expressions, or ambiguous images, clichés, iconographic resources, punctuation, and so on.

Produce and publish news, photo complaints, photo reports, reports, multimedia reports, infographics, news podcasts, interviews, letters to the editor, comments, opinion articles of local or global interest, texts presenting and evaluating cultural productions—reviews and other forms of expression from youth cultures, such as vlogs and cultural podcasts, gameplay, walkthroughs, etc.—and posters, announcements, advertisements, spots, jingles for social campaigns, among others, across various media, while meaningfully experiencing the roles of reporter, commentator, analyst, critic, editor or columnist, booktuber, vlogger, etc., as a way to understand the production conditions that involve the circulation of these texts and to be able to participate and envision possibilities for engagement in the language practices of the journalistic and media fields in an ethical and responsible manner, taking into account the Web 2.0 context, which expands the possibility of circulation of these texts and “blends” the roles of reader and author, consumer and producer.

Produce texts in different genres, taking into account their suitability to the context of production and circulation – the involved speakers, the objectives, the genre, the medium, the circulation – the mode (written or oral; static or moving image, etc.), the appropriate linguistic and/or semiotic variety for that context, and the construction of textuality related to the textual and genre properties, using strategies of planning, drafting, revising, editing, rewriting/redesigning, and evaluating texts. With the help of the teacher and the collaboration of peers, correct and improve the produced works by making cuts, additions, reformulations, and corrections of agreement, spelling, punctuation in texts, and editing images and audio files, making cuts, additions, adjustments, adding or changing effects, ordering, etc.

Review/edit the produced text—news, report, review, opinion article, among others—considering its fit to the production context, the specific media, genre characteristics, textual aspects, the relationship among different semiotic systems, formatting, and proper use of editing tools (text, photo, audio, video, as appropriate) and conformity to standard language.

Plan an advertising campaign on significant issues/problems, themes, or causes for the school and/or community, based on gathering material about the topic or event, defining the target audience, the text or piece to be produced—poster, banner, flyer, leaflet, printed or online advertisement, spot, radio, TV commercial, etc.—the text, audio, or video editing tool to be used, the cut and focus to be given, the persuasion strategies to be employed, and so on.

Produce news for radio, TV, or video, news and opinion podcasts, interviews, commentaries, vlogs, radio and television newspapers, among other possible formats, related to facts and topics of personal, local, or global interest, and oral appreciation and opinion texts – news, cultural, and opinion podcasts and vlogs, guided by a script or text, taking into account the production context and demonstrating mastery of the genres.

Identify and analyze the positions that are defended and refuted when listening to controversial interactions in interviews, discussions, and debates (television, in the classroom, on social media, etc.), among others, and take a stance in response to them.

Develop strategies for planning, drafting, revising, editing, rewriting/redesigning (the last three only when not live) and evaluating oral, audio, and/or video texts, taking into account their suitability to the contexts in which they were produced, the compositional form and genre style, clarity, thematic progression, and linguistic variety used, the speech-related elements such as voice modulation, intonation, rhythm, pitch and intensity, breathing, etc., and the kinesic elements such as body posture, movements and meaningful gestures, facial expression, eye contact with the audience, etc.
Engage and contribute to the search for common conclusions regarding problems, topics, or controversial issues of interest to the class and/or of social relevance.

Formulate questions and break down, with the help of classmates and teachers, a controversial topic or issue, explanations and/or arguments related to the subject of discussion for a more detailed analysis, and seek information or data from various sources that allow you to examine parts of the issue and share them with the class.
Present coherent arguments and counter‑arguments, respecting speaking turns, when participating in discussions about controversial and/or contentious topics.

Analyze and use the compositional forms of journalistic genres in the order of reporting, such as news (inverted pyramid in print versus hypertextual and hypermedia news blocks in digital, which may also include various types of images, videos, audio recordings, etc.), in the order of argumentation, such as opinion pieces and editorials (contextualization, defense of thesis/opinion, and use of arguments), and in interviews: presentation and contextualization of the interviewee and the topic, structure of questions and answers, etc.

Perceive and analyze the stylistic and semiotic resources of journalistic and advertising genres, the aspects related to the treatment of information in news, such as the ordering of events, lexical choices, the effect of impartiality in the report, the verb morphology in news and argumentative texts, recognizing markers of person, number, tense, mood, the distribution of verbs in textual genres (for example, past tense forms in reports; present and future forms in argumentative genres; imperative forms in advertising genres), the use of persuasive resources in various argumentative texts (such as title construction, lexical choices, metaphorical constructions, the explicit or hidden disclosure of information sources), and the strategies of persuasion and appeal to consumption with the linguistic‑discourse resources used (verb tense, word play, metaphors, images).

Use linguistic resources in the writing/rewriting of argumentative texts that mark the sense relationships between paragraphs and sentences and appropriate connective operators for the types of argument and the composition style of argumentative texts, in order to ensure cohesion, coherence, and thematic progression in these texts (“firstly, but, however, in first/second/third place, finally, in conclusion” etc.).
Analyze, in oral genres that involve argumentation, the sense effects of typical spoken modality elements such as pause, intonation, rhythm, gesturality and facial expression, hesitations, etc.

Identify, in view of the production context, the way normative and legal texts are organized, the logic of hierarchy of their items and subitems and their parts: initial part (title – name and date – and summary), blocks of articles (part, book, chapter, section, subsection), articles (head and paragraphs and items) and final part (provisions related to its implementation); and analyze the sense effects caused by the use of technical vocabulary, the use of the imperative, words and expressions indicating circumstances such as adverbs and adverbial phrases, and words indicating generality such as certain indefinite pronouns, in order to understand the imperative, coercive, and general nature of laws and other forms of regulation.

Position oneself in relation to content disseminated in non-institutionalized social participation practices, especially those linked to artistic expressions, cultural productions, urban interventions, and practices specific to youth cultures that aim to denounce, expose a problem, or “call” for reflection/action, relating that text/production to its context of creation and connecting the parts and semiotic elements present for the construction of meaning.

Produce, revise, and edit argumentative or propositional texts about problems that affect school life or the community, justifying viewpoints, claims, and detailing proposals (justification, objectives, planned actions, etc.), taking into account the context of production and the characteristics of the relevant genres.

Contribute to the writing of normative texts when such a demand arises in school—regulations and statutes of civil society organizations that operate in the realm of children and youth (free student council, reading clubs, cultural associations, etc.)—and of rules and regulations in various school contexts—tournaments, festivals, codes of conduct, etc.—taking into account the production context and the characteristics of the relevant genres.

Discuss real or simulated cases subject to judgment that involve alleged violations of ECA articles, the Consumer Defense Code, the National Traffic Code, advertising market regulations, etc., as a way to become familiar with legal texts—their vocabulary, organizational structures, stylistic markers, etc.—in order to facilitate understanding of laws, strengthen rights defense, encourage the writing of normative texts (when and if necessary), and enable comprehension of the interpretive nature of laws and the various perspectives that may be at play.

Position yourself consistently and sustainably in a discussion, assembly, school board meetings, associations, and other situations where proposals are presented and opinions defended, respecting contrary opinions and alternative proposals, and grounding your positions within the allotted speaking time, using clear, justified summaries and proposals.

Take notes during discussions, debates, lectures, proposal presentations, meetings, as a way to document the event and support one's own speech (which may occur during the event or later, for example, when it is necessary to revisit the topics discussed in other public contexts, such as before the represented).

Analyze the compositional structure of texts belonging to normative/legal genres and political sphere genres, such as proposals, political programs (positions on various actions to be proposed, objectives, planned actions, etc.), political propaganda (proposals and their support, positioning on topics under discussion), and advocacy texts: complaint letters, petitions (proposals, their justifications, and actions to be taken) and their linguistic markers, in order to enhance understanding of texts in these genres and to enable the production of more appropriate and/or well-founded texts when required.

Observe the appropriate modalization mechanisms for legal texts, the deontic modalities that refer to the conduct axis (obligation/permissibility), such as: prohibition: “Smoking is not allowed in enclosed spaces.”; obligation: “Life must be worth living.”; possibility: “Entry of minors accompanied by responsible adults is permitted.” and the appropriate modalization mechanisms for political and propositional texts, the evaluative modalities, in which the speaker expresses a value judgment (positive or negative) about what is stated. For example: “What a beautiful speech!” “I disagree with Antônio’s choices.” “Fortunately, the hole has not yet caused more serious accidents.

Reflect on the relationship between the production contexts of scientific communication genres—didactic text, scientific outreach article, scientific outreach report, encyclopedia entry (print and digital), outline, infographic (static and animated), report, multimodal field narrative, podcasts, and various scientific outreach videos, etc.—and the aspects related to compositional construction and the linguistic markers characteristic of these genres, in order to broaden their possibilities for understanding (and producing) texts belonging to these genres.

Compare, with the help of the teacher, contents, data, and information from different sources, taking into account their production contexts and references, identifying coincidences, complementarities, and contradictions, in order to be able to identify conceptual errors/inequalities, understand, and critically position oneself about the contents and information in question.

Use linguistic cues—such as “first/second/third place,” “on the other hand,” “in other words,” “that is,” “for example”—to understand the hierarchy of propositions, summarizing the content of the texts.

Select relevant information and data from various sources (print, digital, oral, etc.), evaluating the quality and usefulness of those sources, and organize, schematically, with the teacher’s help, the necessary information (without exceeding it) with or without digital tools, in charts, tables, or graphs.

Articulate the verbal with schemes, infographics, varied images, etc., in the (re)construction of the meanings of scientific communication texts and retextualize from the discursive to the schematic—infographic, diagram, table, chart, illustration, etc.—and, conversely, transform the content of tables, diagrams, infographics, illustrations, etc., into discursive text, as a way to broaden the possibilities of understanding these texts and to analyze the characteristics of the multisemiotic and the genres in question.

Highlight the essential parts of the text, with the reading objectives in mind, and produce marginalia (or take notes on another medium), organized summaries in bullet points, a synoptic table, a comparative table, a diagram, a summary or review of the text read (with or without commentary/analysis), a concept map, depending on what is most appropriate, as a way to enable greater understanding of the text, the systematization of content and information, and a stance toward the texts, if applicable.

Plan scientific communication texts by first creating a framework that incorporates prior research, notes and summaries of readings, or records of experiments or field studies. Then produce, review, and edit texts aimed at disseminating knowledge, data, and research results—such as a science outreach article, opinion piece, scientific report, encyclopedia entry, collaborative digital encyclopedia entry, infographic, report, scientific experiment narrative, or multimedia field narrative—while considering their production contexts. These contexts may involve making circulating information and knowledge available in a more accessible format for a specific audience or sharing knowledge derived from bibliographic research, scientific experiments, and field studies.

Produce, review, and edit texts aimed at disseminating knowledge and research data and results, such as scientific outreach articles, encyclopedia entries, infographics, animated infographics, scientific podcasts or vlogs, experiment reports, reports, multimodal field reports, among others, taking into account the production context and the regularities of the genres in terms of their compositional structures and styles.

Produce scripts for creating various types of videos (scientific vlog, minute video, radio program, podcasts) to disseminate scientific knowledge and research findings, taking into account their production context, the elements, and the compositional construction of the scripts.

Organize the data and information researched into panels or presentation slides, taking into account the production context, the available time, the characteristics of the oral presentation genre, multisemiotics, the media and technologies that will be used, rehearse the presentation, also considering paralinguistic and kinesic elements, and proceed to orally present the results of studies and research within the allotted time, based on planning and the definition of different ways of using speech – memorized, supported by reading, or spontaneous.

Define the thematic focus of the interview and the interviewee, gather information about the interviewee and the interview topic, develop a questionnaire script, conduct the interview based on the script, allowing for follow‑up questions based on responses when the context permits, take notes, record or save the interview, and appropriately use the information obtained in accordance with the established objectives.
