Analyze, in recordings of seminars, quick conferences, lecture excerpts, and the like, the compositional construction of presentation genres—opening/greeting, introduction to the topic, presentation of the outline, development of the content through the chaining of themes and subthemes (thematic cohesion), final synthesis and/or conclusion, closing—along with paralinguistic elements (such as voice tone and volume, pauses and hesitations—which should generally be minimized, voice modulation and intonation, rhythm, breathing, etc.) and kinesic elements (such as body posture, meaningful movements and gestures, facial expression, eye contact with the audience, voice modulation and intonation, synchronization of speech with supporting tools, etc.) to better perform oral presentations in the field of knowledge dissemination.

Use presentation support tools appropriately, selecting and using font types and sizes that allow good visibility, topicalizing and/or organizing the content into items, inserting images, graphics, tables, shapes and graphic elements correctly, sizing the amount of text (and image) per slide, progressively and harmoniously using more sophisticated resources such as transition effects, master slides, custom layouts, etc.

Analyze the compositional structure of texts belonging to genres related to the dissemination of knowledge: title, eye-catching element, introduction, division of the text into subheadings, illustrative images of concepts, relationships, or complex results (photos, illustrations, schematics, charts, infographics, diagrams, figures, tables, maps, etc.), exposition, containing definitions, descriptions, comparisons, enumerations, examples, and references to concepts and relationships through footnotes, boxes, or links; or title, contextualization of the field, temporal or thematic ordering by theme or subtheme, interleaving of verbal passages with photos, illustrations, audio, video, etc.; and recognize the linguistic traits of scientific outreach texts, consciously using strategies of language impersonality (or personification, if the type of publication and objectives require it, as in some podcasts and science outreach videos), third person, timeless present, use of quotation, use of technical/specialized vocabulary, etc., as a way to broaden your abilities to understand and produce texts in these genres.

Identify and use the ways of introducing other voices into a text—literal quotation and its formatting, and paraphrase—the linguistic cues that signal the author’s and cited authors’ positions in the text (“According to X; As Y states; From my/our perspective, I/we think that” …), and the elements of standardization (such as the rules for including and formatting quotations and paraphrases, and for organizing bibliographic references) in scientific texts, while developing reflection on how intertextuality and retextualization occur in these texts.

Infer the presence of social, cultural, and human values and different worldviews in literary texts, recognizing how these texts establish multiple perspectives on identities, societies, and cultures, while considering the authorship and the social and historical context of their production.

Position oneself critically with respect to texts belonging to genres such as back‑cover blurbs, program notes (for theater, dance, exhibitions, etc.), synopses, critical reviews, blog/vlog cultural commentary, etc., in order to select literary works and other artistic manifestations (film, theater, exhibitions, performances, CDs, DVDs, etc.), distinguishing descriptive and evaluative sequences and recognizing them as genres that support the choice of a book or cultural production, and consulting them at the time of making choices when appropriate.

Participate in reading‑sharing practices and reception of literary works and artistic expressions, such as reading circles, book clubs, storytelling events, dramatic readings, theatrical, musical, and film performances, film clubs, video festivals, literary salons, slams, book‑tube channels, thematic social media groups (for readers, cinephiles, music lovers, etc.), among others, weaving, when possible, aesthetic and affective comments and justifying your appreciations, writing comments and reviews for newspapers, blogs, and social media, and using forms of expression from youth cultures, such as vlogs and cultural podcasts (literature, cinema, theater, music), commented playlists, fan fiction, fanzines, e‑zines, fan videos, fan clips, fanpage posts, honest trailers, video‑minutes, and other possible practices of appreciation and fan culture expression.

Analyze, in fictional narrative texts, the different compositional forms characteristic of each genre, the cohesive devices that construct the passage of time and link its parts, the typical lexical choices of each genre for depicting settings and characters, and the sense effects arising from verb tenses, types of discourse, enunciative verbs, and linguistic varieties (in direct speech, if present) used. Identify the plot and narrative focus, and perceive how the narrative is structured across different genres and the sense effects resulting from the typical narrative focus of each genre, the characterization of physical and psychological spaces and chronological and psychological times, the various voices in the text (narrator, characters in direct and indirect speech), the use of expressive punctuation, connotative words and expressions, figurative processes, and the linguistic‑grammatical resources specific to each narrative genre.

Interpret, in poems, the effects produced by the use of expressive sonic resources (strophing, rhymes, alliterations, etc.), semantic resources (figures of speech, for example), graphic‑spatial resources (distribution of the graphic mark on the paper), images, and their relationship with the verbal text.

Show interest and engagement in reading literature books and other cultural productions from the field, and be receptive to texts that break with your expectations, represent a challenge relative to your current possibilities and previous reading experiences, relying on linguistic cues, your knowledge of genres and themes, and the guidance given by the teacher.

Create a theatrical text by adapting novels, short stories, myths, mystery and adventure narratives, serialized stories, romanticized biographies, chronicles, and others, indicating the guidelines for describing the setting, space, and time; detailing the physical and psychological characterization of the characters and their modes of action; restructuring the use of direct speech and narrator types; specifying linguistic variation markers (dialects, registers, and jargon) and recontextualizing the treatment of the theme.

Engage actively in the processes of planning, drafting, revising/editing, and rewriting, taking into account the thematic, compositional, and stylistic constraints of the intended texts and the configurations of the production situation – the intended reader, the medium, the context of circulation, the purposes, etc. – while considering the imagination, the aesthetic, and the verisimilitude inherent to literary text.

Represent scenes or dramatic texts, taking into account, in the characterization of the characters, the linguistic and paralinguistic aspects of the speech (tone and timbre of voice, pauses and hesitations, intonation and expressiveness, linguistic varieties and registers), the gestures and movements in the stage space, the costume and makeup, and developing the rubrics indicated by the author through the setting, the soundtrack, and the exploration of interpretive modes.

Read aloud a variety of literary texts—such as love stories, humorous pieces, suspense, horror; lyrical, humorous, critical chronicles; as well as chapter‑by‑chapter oral readings (shared or not with the teacher) of longer works like novels, mystery narratives, adventure tales, children’s and young adult literature—telling or retelling stories from both oral tradition (folk tales, clever tales, animal tales, love stories, enchanted tales, jokes, etc.) and written literary tradition, expressing comprehension and interpretation of the text through expressive, fluent reading or speaking that respects the rhythm, pauses, hesitations, and intonation indicated by punctuation and other graphic‑editorial cues such as bold, italics, caps, illustrations, etc. Record this reading or retelling for later analysis, for producing audiobooks of diverse literary texts, or for creating dramatic reading podcasts with or without special effects, and read and/or recite poems in both free and fixed forms (such as quatrains, sonnets, lyric poems, haikus, etc.), using the linguistic, paralinguistic, and kinesic resources needed to achieve the intended meanings—such as rhythm and intonation, use of pauses and elongations, vocal tone and timbre, as well as any gestural or pantomime techniques appropriate to the poetic genre and the sharing situation.

Analyze the sense effects that arise from the interaction between linguistic elements and paralinguistic and kinesic resources, such as variations in rhythm, modulations in vocal tone, pauses, manipulations of the sonic layer of language obtained through strophes, rhymes, and figures of speech like alliterations, assonances, onomatopoeias, among others, bodily posture and gesturality, in the declamation of poems, musical and theatrical performances, both in prose genres and poetic genres; analyze the sense effects that arise from the use of figures of speech such as comparison, metaphor, personification, metonymy, hyperbole, euphemism, irony, paradox, and antithesis; and analyze the sense effects that arise from the use of denotative and connotative words and expressions (adjectives, adjectival phrases, adjectival subordinate clauses, etc.) that function as modifiers, perceiving their role in characterizing the spaces, times, characters, and actions specific to each narrative genre.
Recognize the varieties of spoken language, the concept of a standard norm, and linguistic prejudice.
Use the standard language rules and norms consciously and reflectively in speaking and writing situations where they should be used.

Distinguish different editorial approaches—such as sensationalism, investigative journalism, etc.—in order to identify the techniques used to impact or shock the reader, which may compromise a critical analysis of the news and the reported fact.

Compare news and reports about the same event published in different media, analyzing the specificities of the media, the processes of (re)elaboration of the texts, and the convergence of the media in multisemiotic news or reports.
Create derived words from root words using the most productive prefixes and suffixes in Portuguese.
Recognize, in texts, the verb as the core of sentences.
Identify, in sentences from read texts or one’s own writing, verbs of complete and incomplete predication: intransitive and transitive.
Use the basic rules of nominal and verbal agreement in communicative situations and in text production.
Identify, in read texts or one's own writing, the basic structure of the sentence: subject, predicate, complement (direct and indirect objects).
Identify, in read texts or in one's own writing, adjectives that expand the meaning of the subject noun or verbal complement.
Identify, in read texts or in one’s own writing, adverbs and adverbial phrases that expand the meaning of the clause’s main verb.
Use linguistic and grammatical knowledge when producing text: verb moods and tenses, nominal and verbal agreement, punctuation, etc.

Identify, in read or self‑produced texts, compound sentences in which two clauses are connected by a comma, or by conjunctions that express addition (the conjunction “e”) or opposition (the conjunctions “mas”, “porém”).
Recognize referential cohesion resources: lexical substitutions (replacing nouns with synonyms) or pronominal substitutions (using anaphoric pronouns – personal, possessive, demonstrative).

Establish relationships between parts of the text by identifying lexical substitutions (replacing nouns with synonyms) or pronominal substitutions (using anaphoric pronouns—personal, possessive, demonstrative) that contribute to the continuity of the text.
Identify, in texts, the effects on meaning of using strategies of modalization and argumentation.

Identify and compare the various sections of printed and digital newspapers and news websites, in order to reflect on the types of facts that are reported and commented on, the choices about what to report and what not to report, the emphasis given, and the reliability of the information.
Justify differences or similarities in how the same information is treated in different texts, by consulting fact‑checking websites and services.

Produce opinion articles, given the production context, defending a point of view, using arguments and counter‑arguments and cohesion markers that indicate opposition, contrast, exemplification, and emphasis.
Use linguistic and grammatical knowledge when producing text: spelling, noun and verb agreement and governance, verb moods and tenses, punctuation, etc.
Analyze word‑formation processes by composition (agglutination and juxtaposition), adopting basic hyphen usage rules in compound words.
Identify, in read texts or in one’s own writing, the elements that make up the clause (the subject and its modifiers, the verb and its complements and modifiers).
Differentiate direct and indirect objects of transitive verbs in both read texts and one's own writing, mastering the typical usage patterns of common verbs.
Identify, in read texts or in one’s own writing, verbs in the active and passive voice, interpreting the sense effects of the active and passive subject (the agent of the passive).

Interpret the sense effects of modifiers (adnominal adjuncts – definite or indefinite articles, adjectives, adjectival expressions) in nouns that function as subject or verbal complement, using them to enrich one's own texts.
Interpret the sense effects of verb modifiers (adverbial adjuncts – adverbs and adverbial expressions) in read or self‑produced texts, using them to enrich one's own texts.
Identify, in read texts or one's own writing, the grouping of clauses into sentences, distinguishing coordination from subordination.
Identify subordinate clauses with frequently used conjunctions in read texts, incorporating them into your own productions.
Infer the sense effects that result from using sequential cohesion resources: conjunctions and textual articulators.

Use, when producing text, sequential cohesion devices (linkers) and referential devices (lexical and pronominal), passive and impersonal constructions, direct and indirect discourse, and other expressive resources appropriate to the text genre.
Establish relationships between parts of the text by identifying the antecedent of a relative pronoun or the common referent in a chain of lexical substitutions.
Explain the sense effects of using, in texts, strategies of modalization and argumentativity (punctuation marks, adjectives, nouns, degree expressions, verbs and verbal periphrases, adverbs, etc.).

Analyze the interests that drive the journalistic field, the effects of new technologies on the field, and the conditions that make information a commodity, so as to develop a critical attitude toward journalistic texts.

Analyze different practices (like liking, sharing, commenting, healing, etc.) and texts belonging to various digital culture genres (memes, GIFs, comments, digital cartoons, etc.) involved in handling information and opinion, in order to enable a more critical and ethical presence on social networks.

Analyze opinion texts (opinion articles, editorials, reader letters, comments, blog posts and social media posts, cartoons, memes, gifs, etc.) and position yourself in a critical, well‑grounded, ethical, and respectful manner regarding the facts and opinions related to those texts.

Identify and evaluate explicit and implicit theses/opinions/positions, arguments and counter‑arguments in argumentative texts from the field (letter to the editor, comment, opinion article, critical review, etc.), positioning oneself on the controversial issue in a substantiated manner.
Analyze the effect of meaning produced by the use, in texts, of textual appropriation forms (paraphrases, quotations, direct speech, indirect or free indirect speech).

Analyze the use of persuasive resources in various argumentative texts (such as title creation, lexical choices, metaphorical constructions, the explicit or hidden sources of information) and their effects on meaning.

Analyze, in news, reports, and advertising pieces across various media, the sense effects resulting from the treatment and composition of elements in moving images, the performance, the editing (rhythm, duration, and synchronization between languages – complementarities, interferences, etc.), and the rhythm, melody, instruments, and sampling of music and sound effects.

Plan a print report and other media (radio or TV/video, websites), taking into account the production conditions of the text – purpose, readers/viewers, outlets and circulation media, etc. – based on choosing the fact to be explored or the theme to be focused on (relevant to the class, school, or community), gathering data and information about the fact or theme – which may involve interviews with participants or experts, consulting various sources, analyzing documents, covering events, etc. – recording those information and data, selecting photos or images to produce or use, creating infographics when appropriate, and organizing hypertextual structure (in the case of publishing on news sites or blogs or even printed newspapers, through various boxes).

Produce a printed news report, with a headline, optional byline, compositional organization (expository, interpretive and/or opinionated), thematic progression, and use of linguistic resources compatible with the chosen style and multimedia reports, taking into account production conditions, genre characteristics, available resources and media, its hypertextual organization, and proper handling of audio and image capture and editing resources, while adhering to standard language norms.

Plan opinion pieces, taking into account the conditions of text production—purpose, readers/viewers, outlets and circulation media, etc.—starting from the choice of the topic or issue to be discussed, its relevance to the class, school, or community, gathering data and information about the issue, arguments related to the different positions involved, defining— which may involve consulting various sources, interviewing experts, analyzing texts, schematically organizing information and arguments—the types of arguments and strategies you intend to use to persuade readers.

Produce, review, and edit advertising pieces and campaigns, involving the coordinated and complementary use of different advertising materials: poster, banner, indoor, flyer, leaflet, newspaper/magazine ad, online content, spot, radio, and TV commercials, based on selecting a significant issue/problem/cause for the school and/or school community, defining the target audience, determining the pieces to be produced, and choosing the persuasion and convincing strategies to be used.

Plan collectively the organization of a debate on a pre‑selected topic of collective interest, with agreed rules, and plan, in a group, participation in the debate by gathering information and arguments that can support the position to be defended (which may involve interviewing experts, consulting various sources, recording the obtained information and data, etc.), taking into account the conditions for producing the debate – the profile of the audience and other participants, the objectives of the debate, the motivations for holding it, the most effective arguments and persuasion strategies, etc. and participate in regulated debates, as a member of a debate team, presenter/mediator, spectator (with or without the right to ask questions), and/or judge/evaluator, as a way to understand how a debate works, and to be able to participate convincingly, ethically, respectfully, and critically, developing an attitude of respect and dialogue toward divergent ideas.

Plan oral interviews with people connected to the reported event, specialists, etc., as a way to obtain data and information about the covered facts on the topic or issue discussed or themes under study, taking into account the genre and its production context, starting from gathering information about the interviewee and the theme and from creating a questionnaire, ensuring the relevance of the retained information and thematic continuity, conduct the interview and edit it in audio or video, including an initial contextualization and a closing statement for publishing the interview separately or as part of a multimedia report, adapting it to its publication context and ensuring the relevance of the retained information and thematic continuity.
Analyze, in argumentative and propositional texts, the argumentative movements of support, refutation, and negotiation and the types of arguments, evaluating the strength/type of arguments used.

Use, in debates, argumentative operators that signal the defense of an idea and dialogue with the other’s thesis: I agree, I disagree, I partially agree, from my point of view, from the perspective assumed here, etc.

Analyze the modalization present in news and argumentative texts, through appreciative modalities enabled by grammatical classes and structures such as adjectives, adjectival phrases, adverbs, adverbial phrases, adjectival and adverbial clauses, restrictive and explanatory relative clauses, etc., in order to perceive the ideological appraisal of the reported facts or the implicit or assumed positions.

Relate texts and legal and normative documents of universal, national, or local importance that involve rights, especially those of children, adolescents, and young people—such as the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, the Brazilian Constitution, the Child and Adolescent Statute (ECA)—and the regulation of the school organization—e.g., school bylaws—to their contexts of production, recognizing and analyzing possible motivations, purposes, and their connection to human experiences and historical and social facts, as a way to broaden understanding of rights and duties, to promote democratic principles, and to act guided by the ethics of responsibility (the other has the right to a dignified life just as I do).

Explore and analyze instances and channels of participation available in the school (school council, other committees, student council), in the community (associations, collectives, movements, etc.), in the municipality or country, including digital participation forms such as participation channels and platforms (e.g., e-citizenship portal), services, portals, and tools that track politicians’ work and the passage of laws, political education channels, as well as proposals and propositions circulating in these channels, in order to participate in the debate of ideas and proposals in the social sphere and engage in the search for solutions to problems or issues that involve the life of the school and the community.

Analyze, based on the production context, the way open letters, signatories, and online petitions are organized (identifying the signatories, explicitly stating the claim made, with or without a brief presentation of the problem and/or justifications that support the claim) and the proposal, discussion, and approval of policy proposals or solutions to public interest problems presented or read in digital participation channels, identifying their linguistic features, as a way to enable conscious writing or signing of such letters and texts and to be able to position oneself critically and substantively in front of the proposals.

Compare policy proposals and problem‑solving approaches, identifying what is intended to be done/implemented, why (motivations, justifications), for what (objectives, benefits, and expected consequences), how (actions and steps), when, etc., and the way to evaluate the effectiveness of the proposal/solution, contrasting data and information from different sources, identifying coincidences, complementarities, and contradictions, so as to understand and critically position oneself about the data and information used to support proposals and analyze the coherence among the elements, in order to make informed decisions.

Conduct surveys and opinion polls to identify priorities, problems to solve, or proposals that could improve the school or community; characterize the demand/need, documenting it in various ways through different procedures, genres, and media; and, when appropriate, select relevant information and data from diverse pertinent sources (websites, print, videos, etc.), evaluating the quality and usefulness of these sources to provide context and justification for proposals, cultural projects, and intervention actions.

Understand and compare the different positions and interests at play in a discussion or proposal presentation, evaluating the validity and strength of the arguments and the consequences of what is being proposed, and when appropriate, formulate and negotiate proposals of various kinds related to collective interests involving the school or school community.
Analyze, in argumentative, claim, and proposal texts, the argumentative moves used (support, refutation, and negotiation), evaluating the strength of the arguments used.
Conduct research, defining the scope of the issues, using open and reliable sources.
Disseminate research results through oral presentations, entries in collaborative encyclopedias, science outreach reports, scientific vlogs, various types of videos, etc.

Produce reviews, based on the notes and/or outlines made, with proper handling of the voices involved (the reviewer, the author of the work, and, if applicable, also the authors cited in the reviewed work), through the use of paraphrases, markers of reported speech, and quotations.
Make observations and formulate relevant problematizations at appropriate moments in classroom settings, oral presentations, seminars, etc.

Take notes on video lessons, digital classes, multimedia presentations, science outreach videos, documentaries, and similar materials, identifying, according to the objectives, the main information to support study and, when necessary, producing a final synthesis that highlights and reorganizes the central points or concepts and their relationships, and in some cases, accompanied by personal reflections that may include doubts, questions, considerations, etc.

Use and recognize thematic progression mechanisms, such as anaphoric references (“que, cujo, onde”, nominative and oblique pronouns, demonstrative pronouns, co-referential names, etc.), cataphors (referring forward instead of repeating what has already been said), use of textual organizers, cohesive devices, etc., and analyze the reformulation and paraphrasing mechanisms employed in knowledge dissemination texts.
Analyze the structure of hypertext and hyperlinks in scientific outreach texts circulating on the Web, and refer to concepts and relationships through links.

Analyze and use epistemic modalization, that is, ways of indicating an evaluation of the truth value and truth conditions of a proposition, such as the assertives – when agreeing with (“really, evidently, naturally, effectively, obviously, sure, logical, without doubt” etc.) or disagreeing with (“by no means, in no way”) an idea; and the quasi-assertives, which indicate that the content is considered almost certain (“maybe, like, possibly, probably, eventually”).

Analyze the sense effects that arise from using intertextuality mechanisms (references, allusions, retentions) between literary texts, between those literary texts and other artistic expressions (film, theater, visual and media arts, music), regarding themes, characters, styles, authors, etc., and between the original text and parodies, paraphrases, pastiches, honest trailers, video‑minutes, vidding, among others.

Read independently and understand – selecting appropriate reading procedures and strategies for different purposes and taking into account the characteristics of genres and media – contemporary novels, short stories, micro‑stories, contemporary fables, young adult novels, romantic biographies, novellas, visual chronicles, science‑fiction narratives, suspense narratives, free‑form and fixed‑form poems (such as haiku), concrete poems, cyber‑poems, among others, expressing evaluation of the text read and establishing preferences for genres, themes, and authors.

Analyze the organization of dramatic text presented in theater, television, and cinema, identifying and perceiving the meanings that arise from the linguistic and semiotic resources that support its realization as a theatrical play, soap opera, film, etc.

Create stories or chronicles (especially lyrical), visual chronicles, micro‑stories, adventure and science‑fiction narratives, among others, with themes appropriate to the genre, using knowledge of the structural components and expressive resources typical of the intended narrative genres, and, in the case of group production, collaborative writing tools.

Parody well‑known poems from literature and create texts in verse (such as concrete poems, cyberpoems, haikus, lyric poems, micro‑scripts, lambe‑lambes, and other types of poems), exploring the use of sonic and semantic resources (such as figures of speech and word play) and visual resources (such as relationships between image and verbal text and the distribution of graphic marks), in order to produce different effects of meaning.
Analyze the sense effects of using figures of speech such as irony, euphemism, antithesis, alliteration, assonance, among others.

Analyze the phenomenon of the spread of fake news on social media and develop strategies to recognize them, based on verifying/evaluating the media outlet, source, date and location of publication, authorship, URL, formatting analysis, comparison of different sources, and consulting curation sites that attest to the reliability of the facts and report rumors, etc.
Analyze and comment on the media coverage of socially relevant events, comparing different approaches using curation tools.

Produce opinion articles, given the production context, taking a position on a controversial topic, arguing according to the structure of this type of text and using different kinds of arguments – authority, evidence, exemplification, principle, etc.
Write texts correctly, according to the standard norm, with complex syntactic structures at the clause and sentence level.
Identify, in read texts and in one's own productions, clauses with the subject‑linking verb‑predicative structure.
Differentiate, in read texts and in one's own writings, the sense effect of using the linking verbs “ser,” “estar,” “ficar,” “parecer,” and “permanecer.
Compare the use of verbal and nominal governance in the standard norm with its use in colloquial spoken Brazilian Portuguese.
Identify, in read texts and in one’s own writings, the relationship that coordinating and subordinating conjunctions (and conjunctive phrases) establish between the connected clauses.
Identify the sense effects of using restrictive and explanatory adjective clauses in a compound sentence.
Compare the rules of pronoun placement in the standard norm with their use in colloquial Brazilian Portuguese.
Infer the sense effects resulting from the use of sequential cohesion resources (conjunctions and textual articulators).
Identify foreignisms, characterizing them according to whether or not they preserve their original graphic form, and evaluate the appropriateness, or lack thereof, of their use.
Identify and appreciate distinct forms of traditional and contemporary visual arts, cultivating perception, imagination, the ability to symbolize, and an image repertoire.
Explore and recognize the constitutive elements of visual arts (point, line, shape, color, space, movement, etc.).
Recognize and analyze the influence of distinct aesthetic and cultural matrices of visual arts on artistic manifestations of local, regional, and national cultures.

Experiment with different forms of artistic expression (drawing, painting, collage, comics, origami, sculpture, modeling, installation, video, photography, etc.), using materials, tools, resources, and conventional and non‑conventional techniques sustainably.
Experiment with creating visual arts individually, collectively, and collaboratively, exploring different spaces in the school and the community.
Discuss your own creation and those of your peers, to reach plural meanings.
Recognize some categories of the visual arts system (museums, galleries, institutions, artists, artisans, curators, etc.).
Experiment with and appreciate different forms of dance expressions found in various contexts, developing perception, imagination, the ability to symbolize, and bodily repertoire.
Establish relationships between body parts and between them and the whole body in constructing danced movement.
Experiment with different ways of orienting in space (movements, planes, directions, paths, etc.) and movement rhythms (slow, moderate, and fast) in building the danced movement.

Create and improvise danced movements individually, collectively, and collaboratively, considering the structural, dynamic, and expressive aspects of the constituent elements of movement, based on dance codes.
Discuss, with respect and without prejudice, the personal and collective dance experiences lived in school, as a source for building one's own vocabularies and repertoires.

Identify and critically appreciate diverse forms and genres of musical expression, recognizing and analyzing the uses and functions of music in various circulation contexts, especially those of everyday life.

Perceive and explore the constituent elements of music (pitch, intensity, timbre, melody, rhythm, etc.) through games, play, songs, and various practices of composition/creation, performance, and musical appreciation.

Explore diverse sound sources, such as those in the body itself (claps, voice, body percussion), in nature and everyday objects, recognizing the constitutive elements of music and the characteristics of various musical instruments.

Explore different unconventional musical recording methods (graphical sound representations, creative scores, etc.), as well as audio and audiovisual recording procedures and techniques, and recognize conventional musical notation.

Experiment with improvisations, compositions, and soundscapes for stories, among others, using voices, body sounds, and/or conventional or unconventional musical instruments, individually, collectively, and collaboratively.

Recognize and appreciate distinct forms of theatrical manifestations present in different contexts, learning to see and hear dramatized stories and cultivating perception, imagination, the ability to symbolize, and fictional repertoire.
Discover theatricalities in everyday life, identifying theatrical elements (varied vocal intonations, different physicalities, diversity of characters and narratives, etc.).

Experiment with collaborative, collective, and authorial work in theatrical improvisations and creative narrative processes in theater, exploring from the theatricality of everyday gestures and actions to elements of various aesthetic and cultural matrices.

Exercise imitation and make-believe, re-signifying objects and facts and experimenting in the place of the other, by composing and staging scenic events through music, images, texts, or other starting points, intentionally and reflectively.
Experiment creative possibilities of movement and voice in creating a theatrical character, discussing stereotypes.
Recognize and experience, in thematic projects, the procedural relationships among various artistic languages.
Characterize and experiment with toys, games, dances, songs, and stories from different aesthetic and cultural origins.

Know and appreciate the cultural heritage, both material and immaterial, of diverse cultures, especially Brazilian, including its indigenous, African, and European roots from different eras, fostering the development of vocabulary and repertoire related to various artistic languages.
Explore different technologies and digital resources (multimedia, animations, electronic games, audio and video recordings, photography, software, etc.) in artistic creation processes.

Research, appreciate, and analyze distinct forms of traditional and contemporary visual arts in works by Brazilian and foreign artists from different eras and across various aesthetic and cultural matrices, in order to broaden experience with diverse artistic-visual contexts and practices, and to cultivate perception, imagination, symbolic capacity, and visual repertoire.
Research and analyze different visual styles, contextualizing them in time and space.

Analyze situations in which the languages of visual arts integrate with audiovisual languages (film, animations, videos, etc.), graphic languages (book covers, illustrations of various texts, etc.), scenographic, choreographic, musical, and other related languages.
Analyze the constitutive elements of visual arts (point, line, shape, direction, color, tone, scale, dimension, space, movement, etc.) in the appreciation of different artistic productions.
Experiment with and analyze different forms of artistic expression (drawing, painting, collage, comics, origami, sculpture, modeling, installation, video, photography, performance, etc.).

Develop creation processes in visual arts, based on themes or artistic interests, individually, collectively, and collaboratively, using conventional, alternative, and digital materials, instruments, and resources.
Engage in dialogue with conceptual principles, thematic propositions, visual repertoires, and creative processes in your visual productions.
Differentiate the categories of artist, craftsman, cultural producer, curator, designer, among others, establishing relationships among the professionals in the visual arts system.

Research and analyze different forms of expression, representation, and staging of dance, recognizing and appreciating dance compositions by Brazilian and foreign artists and groups from different eras.
Explore the constitutive elements of everyday movement and choreographed dance, critically addressing the development of dance forms in its traditional and contemporary history.
Experiment with and analyze the movement factors (time, weight, fluency, and space) as elements that, when combined, produce bodily actions and dance movement.
Investigate and experiment with improvisation procedures and movement creation as a source for building one's own vocabularies and repertoires.
Investigate games, collective dances, and other dance practices from different aesthetic and cultural matrices as a reference for creating and composing original dances, individually and in groups.
Analyze and experiment with different elements (costume, lighting, set, soundtrack, etc.) and spaces (conventional and non-conventional) for stage composition and choreographic presentation.
Discuss personal and collective dance experiences encountered at school and in other contexts, questioning stereotypes and prejudices.
