Measure and estimate lengths (including perimeters), masses, and capacities, using the most common standardized units of measurement, valuing and respecting local culture.
Measure, compare, and estimate the area of flat figures drawn on a squared grid by counting whole squares or half-squares, recognizing that two figures with different shapes can have the same area.
Read and record measures and time intervals in hours, minutes, and seconds in situations related to your daily life, such as informing the start and end times of a task and its duration.

Recognize temperature as a quantity and the degree Celsius as the unit of measure associated with it, and use it in comparisons of temperatures in different regions of Brazil or abroad, or in discussions that involve problems related to global warming.
Record the daily maximum and minimum temperatures in everyday locations, and create column charts showing the daily temperature variations, using spreadsheets.
Resolve and create problems that involve buying and selling situations and payment methods, using terms such as change and discount, emphasizing ethical, conscious, and responsible consumption.
Identify, among everyday random events, those that have a higher chance of occurring, recognizing characteristics of more probable outcomes, without using fractions.
Analyze data presented in simple tables or two‑way tables and in column or pictorial graphs, based on information from different knowledge areas, and produce a text that synthesizes your analysis.
Conduct research involving categorical and numerical variables and organize collected data using simple or grouped column tables and charts, with and without digital technologies.
Read, write, and order natural numbers up to the hundred‑thousand place while understanding the main characteristics of the decimal numbering system.
Read, write, and order rational numbers in decimal form, understanding the main characteristics of the decimal numbering system, using composition and decomposition and the number line as resources.
Identify and represent fractions (both less than and greater than one), associating them with the result of a division or the idea of a part of a whole, using the number line as a resource.
Identify equivalent fractions.
Compare and order positive rational numbers (fractional and decimal representations), relating them to points on the number line.

Associate the representations 10%, 25%, 50%, 75% and 100% respectively with the tenth part, quarter, half, three quarters and one whole, in order to calculate percentages, using personal strategies, mental calculation and calculator, in contexts of financial education, among others.

Solve and create addition and subtraction problems with natural numbers and with rational numbers whose decimal representation is finite, using various strategies such as estimation, mental calculation, and algorithms.

Resolve and create multiplication and division problems with natural numbers and with rational numbers whose decimal representation is finite (using a natural multiplier and a natural divisor different from zero), employing various strategies such as estimation, mental calculation, and algorithms.

Resolve and formulate simple counting problems involving the multiplicative principle, such as determining the number of possible groupings when combining each element of one collection with all elements of another collection, using tree diagrams or tables.

Conclude, through investigations, that the equality relationship between two terms remains when adding, subtracting, multiplying, or dividing each of those terms by the same number, in order to build the notion of equivalence.
Solve and create problems whose conversion into a mathematical statement is an equality with an operation in which one of the terms is unknown.

Solve problems that involve direct proportionality between two quantities, to associate the amount of a product with the value to pay, to change the quantities of ingredients in recipes, to enlarge or reduce scale in maps, among others.

Solve problems that involve dividing a quantity into two unequal parts, such as splitting a quantity into two parts so that one part is twice the other, with an understanding of the idea of the ratio between the parts and the whole.

Use and understand different representations for locating objects in the plane, such as maps, cells in spreadsheets, and geographic coordinates, in order to develop the first notions of Cartesian coordinates.

Interpret, describe, and represent the location or movement of objects in the Cartesian plane (first quadrant), using Cartesian coordinates, indicating changes in direction and sense as well as turns.
Associate spatial figures with their plans (prisms, pyramids, cylinders, and cones) and analyze, name, and compare their attributes.
Recognize, name, and compare polygons, considering sides, vertices, and angles, and draw them using drawing materials or digital technologies.
Recognize the congruence of angles and the proportionality between corresponding sides of polygonal figures in situations of enlargement and reduction in grid meshes and using digital technologies.

Resolve and elaborate problems involving measurements of the quantities length, area, mass, time, temperature, and capacity, using transformations between the most common units in sociocultural contexts.
Conclude, through investigations, that figures with equal perimeters can have different areas, and also that figures with the same area can have different perimeters.
Recognize volume as a quantity associated with geometric solids and measure volumes by stacking cubes, preferably using concrete objects.
Present all possible outcomes of a random experiment, estimating whether these outcomes are equally likely or not.
Determine the probability of a result occurring in random events when all possible outcomes have an equal chance of occurring (equiprobable).

Interpret statistical data presented in texts, tables, and column or line graphs, related to other areas of knowledge or other contexts such as health and traffic, and produce texts with the goal of synthesizing conclusions.

Conduct research involving categorical and numerical variables, organize collected data using tables, column charts, pictograms, and line graphs, with or without digital technologies, and present a written text explaining the purpose of the research and summarizing the results.
Compare, order, read, and write natural numbers and rational numbers whose decimal representation is finite, using the number line.

Recognize the decimal numbering system, as it prevailed in the Western world, and highlight similarities and differences with other systems, in order to systematize its main characteristics (base, positional value, and the function of zero), including the composition and decomposition of natural numbers and rational numbers in their decimal representation.

Solve and create problems that involve calculations (mental or written, exact or approximate) with natural numbers, using varied strategies, with an understanding of the processes involved both with and without a calculator.
Build an algorithm in natural language and represent it with a flowchart that shows the solution to a simple problem (for example, whether any natural number is even).

Classify natural numbers as prime or composite, establish relationships between numbers expressed by the terms “is a multiple of,” “is a divisor of,” “is a factor of,” and, through investigations, establish divisibility criteria for 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10, 100, and 1000.
Solve and create problems that involve the concepts of multiple and divisor.
Understand, compare, and order fractions related to the concepts of parts of whole numbers and the result of division, identifying equivalent fractions.

Recognize that positive rational numbers can be expressed in fractional and decimal forms, establish relationships between these representations, convert from one representation to another, and relate them to points on the number line.
Solve and create problems that involve calculating the fraction of a quantity and whose result is a natural number, with and without using a calculator.
Solve and create problems that involve addition or subtraction with positive rational numbers in fractional representation.

Solve and create problems involving positive rational numbers in decimal form, using the four basic operations and exponentiation, through various strategies, and using estimates and rounding to check the reasonableness of answers, with and without a calculator.
Make estimates of quantities and round numbers to the nearest multiple of a power of 10.

Solve and create problems involving percentages, based on the idea of proportionality, without using the “rule of three,” using personal strategies, mental calculation, and calculator, in contexts of financial education, among others.

Recognize that the mathematical equality relation does not change when adding, subtracting, multiplying, or dividing its two members by the same number and use this notion to determine unknown values in problem solving.

Solve and formulate problems that involve sharing a quantity into two unequal parts, involving additive and multiplicative relationships, as well as the ratio between the parts and between one part and the whole.
Associate ordered pairs of numbers with points in the first quadrant of the Cartesian plane, in situations such as locating the vertices of a polygon.
Quantify and establish relationships between the number of vertices, faces, and edges of prisms and pyramids, as a function of their base polygon, to solve problems and develop spatial perception.
Recognize, name, and compare polygons, considering sides, vertices, and angles, and classify them as regular and irregular, both in their representations in the plane and in faces of polyhedra.
Identify the characteristics of triangles and classify them based on the measurements of their sides and angles.
Identify the characteristics of quadrilaterals, classify them according to their sides and angles, and recognize the inclusion and intersection of classes among them.
Construct similar flat figures in situations of enlargement and reduction, using graph paper, a Cartesian plane, or digital technologies.
Use tools such as rulers and compasses, or software, to represent parallel and perpendicular lines and to construct quadrilaterals, among others.

Build an algorithm to solve step‑by‑step situations (such as in the construction of folds or in indicating the displacement of an object in the plane according to reference points and provided distances, etc.).

Solve and create problems involving the quantities length, mass, time, temperature, area (triangles and rectangles), capacity, and volume (solids formed by rectangular blocks), without using formulas, always, when possible, placing them in contexts derived from real situations and/or related to other areas of knowledge.
Recognize the opening of an angle as a magnitude associated with geometric figures.
Solve problems that involve the notion of angle in different contexts and in real situations, such as field of view.
Determine the measures of angles using a protractor and/or digital technologies.
Interpret, describe, and draw simple floor plans of residences and aerial views.

Analyze and describe the changes that occur in the perimeter and area of a square when its side lengths are increased or decreased, in order to understand that the perimeter is proportional to the side length, which does not happen with the area.

Calculate the probability of a random event, expressing it as a rational number (fractional, decimal, and percentage form) and compare that number with the probability obtained through successive experiments.
Identify the variables and their frequencies and the constitutive elements (title, axes, legends, sources, and dates) in different types of graphs.

Interpret and solve situations that involve data from research on environmental contexts, sustainability, traffic, responsible consumption, among others, presented by the media in tables and in different types of graphs, and write texts with the objective of synthesizing conclusions.
Plan and collect research data on social practices chosen by students and use electronic spreadsheets to record, represent, and interpret the information in tables, various types of graphs, and text.

Interpret and develop simple flowcharts, identifying the relationships between the represented objects (for example, the position of cities considering the roads that connect them, the hierarchy of employees in a company, etc.).

Resolve and create problems involving natural numbers, including concepts of divisor and multiple, possibly incorporating greatest common divisor or least common multiple, using various strategies without applying algorithms.

Resolve and create problems involving percentages, such as those dealing with simple increases and decreases, using personal strategies, mental calculation and calculator, in the context of financial education, among others.
Compare and order integer numbers in different contexts, including the historical, associate them with points on the number line, and use them in situations that involve addition and subtraction.
Solve and create problems that involve operations with integers.
Solve the same problem using different algorithms.
Recognize that the solutions of a group of problems that have the same structure can be obtained using the same procedures.
Represent the steps used to solve a set of problems using a flowchart.
Compare and order fractions related to the concepts of parts of wholes, results of division, ratio, and operator.

Use, when solving problems, the link between ratio and fraction, such as the fraction 2/3 to express the ratio of two parts of a quantity to three parts of the same quantity or three parts of another quantity.
Compare and order rational numbers in different contexts and associate them with points on the number line.
Understand and use the multiplication and division of rational numbers, the relationship between them, and their operational properties.
Solve and create problems that involve operations with rational numbers.
Understand the concept of a variable, represented by a letter or symbol, to express the relationship between two quantities, distinguishing it from the concept of an unknown.
Classify sequences as recursive and non-recursive, recognizing that the concept of recursion is present not only in mathematics, but also in the arts and literature.
Use algebraic symbolism to express regularities found in numerical sequences.
Recognize whether two algebraic expressions obtained to describe the regularity of the same numerical sequence are or are not equivalent.
Resolve and formulate problems that involve direct proportionality and inverse proportionality between two quantities, using an algebraic sentence to express the relationship between them.
Solve and create problems that can be represented by first‑degree polynomial equations, reducible to the form ax + b = c, using the properties of equality.
Perform transformations of polygons represented in the Cartesian plane, resulting from multiplying the coordinates of their vertices by an integer.
Recognize and represent, in the Cartesian plane, the symmetric of figures with respect to the axes and the origin.

Recognize and construct figures obtained by symmetries of translation, rotation, and reflection, using drawing instruments or dynamic geometry software, and link this study to planar representations of works of art, architectural elements, among others.
Build circles using a compass, recognize them as a geometric locus, and use them to create artistic compositions and solve problems involving equidistant objects.
Verify relationships between the angles formed by parallel lines cut by a transversal, with and without the use of dynamic geometry software.

Construct triangles using a ruler and compass, recognize the condition for a triangle’s existence based on the lengths of its sides, and verify that the sum of the measures of a triangle’s interior angles is 180°.
Recognize the geometric rigidity of triangles and their applications, such as in the construction of architectural structures (roofs, metal structures and others) or in the visual arts.
Describe, in writing and using a flowchart, an algorithm for constructing any triangle when the lengths of its three sides are known.

Calculate the measures of internal angles of regular polygons without using formulas, and establish relationships between the internal and external angles of polygons, preferably in connection with the construction of mosaics and tilings.
Describe, in writing and through a flowchart, an algorithm for constructing a regular polygon (such as a square or equilateral triangle) given the length of its side.

Solve and create problems that involve measurements of quantities placed in contexts derived from everyday situations or other areas of knowledge, recognizing that every empirical measurement is approximate.
Solve and create problems involving the calculation of the volume of rectangular blocks, using the usual units (cubic meter, cubic decimeter, and cubic centimeter).
Establish expressions for calculating the area of triangles and quadrilaterals.
Solve and create problems involving the calculation of the area of flat figures that can be decomposed into squares, rectangles, and/or triangles, using the equivalence between areas.
Establish the number π as the ratio between the measure of a circumference and its diameter, in order to understand and solve problems, including those of historical nature.
Plan and conduct random experiments or simulations that involve calculating probabilities or estimating them through occurrence frequencies.
Understand, in meaningful contexts, the meaning of the statistical mean as an indicator of a study’s tendency, calculate its value, and intuitively relate it to the spread of the data set.

Plan and conduct research involving a social reality theme, identifying whether a census or a sample is needed, and interpret the data to communicate them through a written report, tables, and graphs, with the support of electronic spreadsheets.
Interpret and analyze data presented in pie charts published by the media and understand when it is possible or convenient to use them.
Perform calculations with powers of integer exponents and apply that knowledge to represent numbers in scientific notation.
Solve and create problems using the relationship between exponentiation and root extraction, to represent a root as a power with a fractional exponent.
Solve and create counting problems whose solution involves the application of the multiplicative principle.
Solve and create problems involving percentage calculations, including the use of digital technologies.
Recognize and use procedures to obtain a generating fraction for a repeating decimal.
Solve and create problems that involve calculating the numerical value of algebraic expressions, using the properties of operations.
Associate a first‑degree linear equation with two unknowns to a line in the Cartesian plane.

Resolve and create problems related to your immediate context that can be represented by systems of first‑degree equations with two unknowns, and interpret them, using the Cartesian plane as a resource.
Solve and create, with and without the use of technologies, problems that can be represented by second‑degree polynomial equations of the form ax² = b.
Identify the regularity of a non‑recursive numerical or figurative sequence and construct an algorithm using a flowchart that allows you to indicate the following numbers or figures.
Identify the regularity of a recursive numerical sequence and construct an algorithm using a flowchart that allows indicating the subsequent numbers.

Identify the nature of the variation between two quantities—whether directly proportional, inversely proportional, or not proportional—expressing the relationship with an algebraic statement and representing it on the Cartesian plane.
Solve and create problems that involve quantities that are directly or inversely proportional, using a variety of strategies.
Demonstrate properties of quadrilaterals by identifying triangle congruence.
Build, using drawing instruments or dynamic geometry software, perpendicular bisectors, angle bisectors, 90°, 60°, 45°, and 30° angles, and regular polygons.
Describe, in writing and via a flowchart, an algorithm for constructing a regular hexagon of any area, based on the measure of the central angle and using rulers and compasses.
Apply the concepts of perpendicular bisector and angle bisector as geometric loci in problem solving.
Recognize and construct figures obtained by compositions of geometric transformations (translation, reflection, and rotation), using drawing instruments or dynamic geometry software.

Solve and create problems that involve measuring the area of geometric figures, using area calculation expressions (quadrilaterals, triangles, and circles), in situations such as determining the size of land plots.
Recognize the relationship between a liter and a cubic decimeter and the relationship between a liter and a cubic meter, in order to solve problems involving the calculation of container capacities.
Solve and create problems that involve calculating the volume of a container whose shape is that of a rectangular block.

Calculate the probability of events, based on the construction of the sample space, using the multiplicative principle, and recognize that the sum of the probabilities of all elements of the sample space equals 1.
Evaluate the suitability of different types of graphs to represent a data set from a survey.
Classify the frequencies of a continuous variable from a survey into classes so that the data are summarized appropriately for decision making.
Obtain the values of measures of central tendency of a statistical survey (mean, mode, and median) with an understanding of their meanings and relate them to data dispersion, indicated by the range.

Select reasons, of different natures (physical, ethical, or economic), that justify conducting sample and non-census research, and recognize that sample selection can be done in different ways (simple random, systematic, and stratified).

Plan and execute a sample survey, selecting an appropriate sampling technique, and write a report that includes the appropriate graphs to represent the data sets, highlighting aspects such as measures of central tendency, range, and conclusions.

Recognize that, once a unit of length is fixed, there are line segments whose length is not expressed by a rational number (such as the measures of diagonals of a polygon and heights of a triangle, when each side is taken as the unit).
Recognize an irrational number as a real number whose decimal representation is infinite and non‑periodic, and estimate the location of some of them on the number line.
Perform calculations with real numbers, including powers with fractional exponents.
Solve and create problems with real numbers, including scientific notation, involving different operations.

Solve and create problems involving percentages, with the idea of applying successive percentages and determining percentage rates, preferably using digital technologies, in the context of financial education.

Understand functions as one-to-one dependency relationships between two variables and their numerical, algebraic, and graphical representations, and use this concept to analyze situations involving functional relationships between two variables.
Solve problems that involve the ratio between two quantities of different types, such as speed and population density.

Resolve and formulate problems that involve direct and inverse proportionality relationships between two or more quantities, including scales, division into proportional parts, and rate of change, in sociocultural, environmental, and other contexts.

Understand the processes of factoring algebraic expressions, based on their relationships with special products, to solve and create problems that can be represented by quadratic polynomial equations.
Show simple relationships between the angles formed by parallel lines cut by a transversal.
Solve problems by establishing relationships between arcs, central angles, and inscribed angles on the circle, including the use of dynamic geometry software.
Recognize the necessary and sufficient conditions for two triangles to be similar.
Demonstrate metric relationships of the right triangle, including the Pythagorean theorem, using, among other methods, triangle similarity.
Solve and create application problems involving the Pythagorean theorem or proportionality relationships with parallel lines cut by secants.
Describe, in writing and through a flowchart, an algorithm for constructing a regular polygon whose side length is known, using a ruler and compass, as well as software.

Determine the midpoint of a line segment and the distance between any two points, given the coordinates of those points in the Cartesian plane, without using formulas, and use this knowledge to calculate, for example, measurements of perimeters and areas of planar figures constructed in the plane.
Recognize orthogonal views of spatial figures and apply that knowledge to draw objects in perspective.

Recognize and use units used to express very large or very small measures, such as the distance between planets and solar systems, the size of viruses or cells, computer storage capacity, among others.
Solve and create problems involving measurements of volumes of prisms and right cylinders, including the use of calculation expressions, in everyday situations.
Recognize, in random experiments, independent and dependent events and calculate the probability of their occurrence, in both cases.

Analyze and identify, in graphs published by the media, the elements that can sometimes deliberately induce reading errors, such as inappropriate scales, improperly explained legends, omission of important information (sources and dates), among others.

Choose and construct the most appropriate graph (columns, sectors, lines), with or without the use of spreadsheets, to present a given set of data, highlighting aspects such as measures of central tendency.

Plan and execute a sample research involving a theme of social reality and communicate the results through a report containing an evaluation of measures of central tendency and spread, appropriate tables and graphs, constructed with the support of electronic spreadsheets.
Compare the characteristics of different materials found in everyday objects, discussing their origins, how they are discarded, and how they can be used more consciously.
Locate, name, and graphically represent (through drawings) parts of the human body and explain their functions.
Discuss the reasons why body hygiene habits (washing hands before eating, brushing teeth, cleaning the eyes, nose, and ears, etc.) are necessary for maintaining health.
Compare physical characteristics among peers, recognizing diversity and the importance of valuing, welcoming, and respecting differences.
Identify and name different time scales: the daily periods (morning, afternoon, evening) and the succession of days, weeks, months, and years.
Select examples of how the succession of days and nights guides the rhythm of daily activities of humans and other living beings.
Identify what materials (metals, wood, glass, etc.) everyday objects are made of, how these objects are used, and what materials were used to produce them in the past.
Propose the use of different materials for building everyday objects, taking into account some properties of those materials (flexibility, hardness, transparency, etc.).
Discuss the necessary precautions for preventing domestic accidents (sharp objects and flammable items, electricity, cleaning products, medications, etc.).

Describe the characteristics of plants and animals (size, shape, color, life stage, location where they develop, etc.) that are part of your daily life and relate them to the environment in which they live.
Investigate the importance of water and light for the maintenance of plant life in general.

Identify the main parts of a plant (root, stem, leaves, flowers, and fruits) and the function performed by each, and analyze the relationships between plants, the environment, and other living beings.
Describe the positions of the Sun at various times of day and associate them with the size of the projected shadow.
Compare the effect of solar radiation (heating and reflection) on different types of surfaces (water, sand, soil, dark, light, metallic, etc.).
Produce different sounds from the vibration of various objects and identify variables that influence this phenomenon.

Experiment and report what happens when light passes through transparent objects (cups, glass windows, lenses, prisms, water, etc.), when it contacts polished surfaces (mirrors), and when it intersects opaque objects (walls, plates, people, and other everyday objects).
Discuss the habits necessary for maintaining auditory and visual health, taking into account environmental conditions in terms of sound and light.
Identify characteristics about the way of life (what they eat, how they reproduce, how they move, etc.) of the most common animals in the nearby environment.
Describe and communicate the changes that occur from birth in animals of different terrestrial or aquatic environments, including humans.
Compare some animals and organize groups based on common external characteristics (presence of feathers, fur, scales, beak, claws, antennae, legs, etc.).

Identify characteristics of Earth (such as its spherical shape, presence of water, soil, etc.) based on observation, manipulation, and comparison of different representations of the planet (maps, globes, photographs, etc.).
Observe, identify, and record the daily periods (day and/or night) during which the Sun, other stars, the Moon, and planets are visible in the sky.
Compare different soil samples from around the school based on characteristics such as color, texture, smell, particle size, permeability, etc.
Identify the different uses of soil (planting and extraction of materials, among other possibilities), recognizing the importance of soil for agriculture and for life.
Identify mixtures in everyday life based on their observable physical properties, recognizing their composition.
Test and report changes in everyday materials when exposed to different conditions (heating, cooling, light, and humidity).
Conclude that some changes caused by heating or cooling are reversible (such as the physical state changes of water) and others are not (such as cooking an egg, burning paper, etc.).
Analyze and construct simple food chains, recognizing the position occupied by living organisms in those chains and the role of the Sun as the primary source of energy in food production.
Describe and highlight the similarities and differences between the matter cycle and the energy flow among the living and non‑living components of an ecosystem.
Relate the participation of fungi and bacteria in the decomposition process, recognizing the environmental importance of this process.
Verify the participation of microorganisms in the production of foods, fuels, medicines, among others.
Propose, based on knowledge of the transmission methods of certain microorganisms (viruses, bacteria, and protozoa), appropriate attitudes and measures for preventing diseases associated with them.
Identify the cardinal points, based on the record of different relative positions of the Sun and the shadow of a stick (gnomon).
Compare the indications of the cardinal points obtained by observing the shadows of a stick (gnomon) with those obtained using a compass.
Associate the cyclical movements of the Moon and Earth with regular time periods and use that knowledge to construct calendars in different cultures.

Explore everyday life phenomena that demonstrate the physical properties of materials – such as density, thermal and electrical conductivity, responses to magnetic forces, solubility, responses to mechanical forces (hardness, elasticity, etc.), among others.

Apply knowledge of the physical state changes of water to explain the hydrological cycle and analyze its implications for agriculture, climate, electricity generation, potable water supply, and the balance of regional (or local) ecosystems.
Select arguments that justify the importance of vegetation cover for the maintenance of the water cycle, soil conservation, watercourses, and atmospheric air quality.
Identify the main uses of water and other materials in everyday activities in order to discuss and propose sustainable ways of using these resources.
Build collective proposals for more conscious consumption and create technological solutions for proper disposal and reuse or recycling of materials consumed in school and/or everyday life.
Select arguments that justify why the digestive and respiratory systems are considered co‑responsible for the organism’s nutrition process, based on identifying the functions of these systems.
Justify the relationship between how the circulatory system works, the distribution of nutrients throughout the body, and the elimination of produced waste.
Organize a balanced menu based on the characteristics of food groups (nutrients and calories) and individual needs (activities performed, age, sex, etc.) to maintain the health of the body.

Discuss the occurrence of nutritional disorders (such as obesity, undernutrition, etc.) among children and adolescents by analyzing their habits (types and amount of food consumed, physical activity practice, etc.).
Identify some constellations in the sky, using resources such as star charts and digital apps, and the times of year when they are visible at the beginning of the evening.
Associate the daily movement of the Sun and other stars in the sky with the Earth's rotation.
Conclude about the periodicity of the Moon’s phases, based on observing and recording the apparent shapes of the Moon in the sky over at least two months.

Design and build devices for distant observation (lup, periscope, etc.), for enlarged observation of objects (magnifying glasses, microscopes), or for image recording (photographic cameras), and discuss the social uses of these devices.
Classify a mixture of two or more materials (water and salt, water and oil, water and sand, etc.) as homogeneous or heterogeneous.

Identify evidence of chemical transformations from the result of mixing materials that produce products different from those that were mixed (e.g., mixing ingredients to make a cake, mixing vinegar with baking soda, etc.).

Select the most appropriate methods for separating different heterogeneous systems based on identifying material separation processes (such as table salt production, petroleum distillation, among others).
Associate the production of medicines and other synthetic materials with scientific and technological development, recognizing benefits and evaluating socio-environmental impacts.
Explain the basic organization of cells and their role as the structural and functional unit of living beings.
Conclude, based on the analysis of illustrations and/or models (physical or digital), that organisms are a complex arrangement of systems with different levels of organization.
Justify the role of the nervous system in coordinating the body's motor and sensory actions, based on an analysis of its basic structures and respective functions.

Explain the importance of vision (capturing and interpreting images) in the organism’s interaction with the environment and, based on how the human eye works, select appropriate lenses to correct different vision defects.
Deduce that the structure, support, and movement of animals result from the interaction between the muscular, skeletal, and nervous systems.
Explain how the functioning of the nervous system can be affected by psychoactive substances.
Identify the different layers that structure the planet Earth (from the internal structure to the atmosphere) and their main characteristics.
Identify different types of rock, relating the formation of fossils to sedimentary rocks in different geological periods.
Select arguments and evidence that demonstrate the Earth's sphericity.

Infer that the changes in the shadow of a gnomon throughout the day at different times of the year are evidence of the relative movements between the Earth and the Sun, which can be explained by the Earth's rotation and orbital motion and the tilt of its axis relative to the plane of its orbit around the Sun.
Discuss the application, throughout history, of simple machines and propose solutions and inventions for performing everyday mechanical tasks.
Differentiate temperature, heat, and thermal sensation in various everyday thermodynamic equilibrium situations.

Use knowledge of heat propagation methods to justify the use of specific materials (conductors and insulators) in everyday life, explain the operating principle of certain devices (thermos flask, solar collector, etc.), and/or develop technological solutions based on that knowledge.
Evaluate the role of thermodynamic equilibrium for the maintenance of life on Earth, for the operation of thermal machines, and in other everyday situations.

Discuss the use of different types of fuel and thermal machines over time, to evaluate advances, economic issues, and socio‑environmental problems caused by the production and use of these materials and machines.

Discuss and evaluate economic, cultural, and social changes, both in everyday life and in the world of work, resulting from the development of new materials and technologies (such as automation and informatization).

Characterize the main Brazilian ecosystems in terms of landscape, amount of water, type of soil, availability of sunlight, temperature, etc., correlating these characteristics with specific flora and fauna.

Evaluate how the impacts caused by natural disasters or changes in the physical, biological, or social components of an ecosystem affect its populations, potentially threatening or causing species extinction, altering habits, migration, etc.

Interpret the health conditions of a community, city, or state by analyzing and comparing health indicators (such as infant mortality rate, basic sanitation coverage, incidence of waterborne and airborne diseases, among others) and the outcomes of public health policies.

Argue about the importance of vaccination for public health, based on information about how vaccines work in the body and the historical role of vaccination in maintaining individual and collective health and eradicating diseases.
Analyze historically the use of technology, including digital technology, in the different dimensions of human life, taking into account environmental and quality-of-life indicators.
Show that air is a mixture of gases, identify its composition, and discuss natural or anthropogenic phenomena that can alter that composition.

Describe the natural mechanism of the greenhouse effect, its fundamental role for the development of life on Earth, discuss the human actions responsible for its artificial increase (burning fossil fuels, deforestation, fires, etc.), and select and implement proposals to reverse or control this situation.

Explain why the ozone layer is important for life on Earth, identify the factors that increase or decrease its presence in the atmosphere, and discuss individual and collective proposals for its preservation.
Interpret natural phenomena (such as volcanoes, earthquakes, and tsunamis) and justify the rare occurrence of these phenomena in Brazil, based on the tectonic plate model.
Justify the shape of the Brazilian and African coastlines based on the theory of continental drift.
Identify and classify different sources (renewable and non-renewable) and types of energy used in homes, communities, or cities.
Build electrical circuits using a battery, wires, a light bulb or other devices, and compare them to residential electrical circuits.

Classify residential electrical equipment (shower, iron, lamps, TV, radio, refrigerator, etc.) according to the type of energy transformation (from electrical energy to thermal, luminous, sound, and mechanical, for example).

Calculate the consumption of household appliances from the power data (described on the appliance itself) and average usage time to evaluate the impact of each appliance on monthly household consumption.

Propose collective actions to optimize the use of electric energy in your school and/or community, based on selecting equipment according to sustainability criteria (energy consumption and energy efficiency) and responsible consumption habits.

Discuss and evaluate electric power generation plants (thermal, hydroelectric, wind, etc.), their similarities and differences, their socio‑environmental impacts, and how that energy reaches and is used in your city, community, home, or school.
Compare different reproductive processes in plants and animals in relation to adaptive and evolutionary mechanisms.
Analyze and explain the transformations that occur during puberty, considering the action of sex hormones and the nervous system.

Compare the mode of action and effectiveness of various contraceptive methods and justify the need to share responsibility in choosing and using the most appropriate method for preventing early and unwanted pregnancy and sexually transmitted diseases.
Identify the main symptoms, modes of transmission, and treatment of certain STDs (with an emphasis on AIDS), and discuss strategies and methods of prevention.
